Although it is the intention of the Government and the South African Committee to call Mr. Rhodes 113 f,ht l first witness, and Mr. Chamberlain in send- ing him an invitation, it must not be overlooked that Mr. Rhodes has to satisfy himself that the evidence he may give will not be used against him in some prosecution afterwards. From private in- formation which reached us a few weeks ago, I was able to say that he was seeking and had not then received, assurances on the point. If they are go- ing out in Mr. Chamberlain's letter, all will be well, and Mr. Rhodes will be here again in January; but if they are not his answer will not be immedi- ate, and it may not be in the affirmative.

It is a significant fact that the past menth,which has.seen all the millionaires of the Rand enjoying themselves in Europe, and busily informing their favourite organs that Mr. Kruger's policy has ruined the trade of the Transvaal, has shown a record output for the industries of that favoured land.

It has been stated that the German Emperor's latest fad is billiard playing, and that on returning from Norway he ordered a table to be specially made and sent to Wilhelmshii he where, by the way he lived when at school in Cassel. But there must surely be some mistake here. For the Emperor. as is well known, has no power whatever in his left hand—with which therefore, he could not possibly, steady or support his cue; and we have never yet heard of a one-armed billiard player.

Dr. Nausea is the hero of the hour in scientific circles, and as the Royal Geographical Society does not meet for some time the efforts to draw him to the British Association will, it is believed, be suc- cessful. The number of eminent men who have been at different times attracted to the British Association at the beginning of a famous career is very considerable. 'The general theory was ex- pounded in this way, and Dr. Nansen will be none the less welcome that he has probably more new facts to communicate than theories. The invita- tion sent to him cannot receive an answer for several days.

The new London coal ring will apparently soon be in working order. Although it was first announced as a cc mbination for the protection of consumers, it turns out to be in a great measure a middleman's movement, though some large firms of middlemen have not yet identified themselves with it. The first proof of how little it is a consumers' protective society is shown in the fact that one of the first actions of the syndicate will be to restrict the import of coal into the metropolis, which means of course, a raising of the price to the public. To this arrangement the great coalowners will be a party. So far as can be seen at present, the sole advantage which the public will derive from the forroation of the syndicate will be that London will henchforth be the victim of two rings instead of one, and that if there is competition between them, and a fair amount of business jealously, the rapacity of the one ring will be checked by the competitive eagerness of the other; but the probability rather is that,tas the syndicate has already sucked into its vortex some of the very largest coal-distributing firms in London, those that still hold aloof will soon be drawn into it also.

Intently as the Cretan question is being watche d as far as operation in the island and the varying mood of the Sultan are concerned, the new point of interest is Paris, whence como some very significant intimations of a disposition to promote a better understanding with this country,which may or may not be of Russian inspiration. French journalists in town do not attribute them to this cause so much as to growing disgust with the cruelties of the Turks, and a strong desire to bring to an end the impotence of the Powers. Whatever the cause may be, it is most agreeable to find that a good deal of the old bitter feeling against doing anything with this country even in the most humane efforts is gradually passing away It is to this change of sentiment that much of the cynical comments in Germany and Austria are due, and it is from their journals we first had news of the failure of the Ruaopean blockade of Crete.

Li Chung Tong's interpreters have a very difficult task, Ravi the " Chronicle," in repeating literally all that tie Excellency desires to say. Mr. Lo Feng- Luh nearly always gives each. question or remark faithfully, but 14e acknowledges that on several occasions he has been obliged to slightly alter and miadify his Excellency's meaning. For instance, there was a period, when Li Chung Tong was fond of humorously oSserving that the person with whom be Was coniersing was drunk or was a drunkard! Mr. Lo Feng-Luh,knowing that the criticism would be taken as an insult, although no offence was meant, generally translated it as " The Viceroy says you are intoxicated with success !" On one occas- ion, *however, the actual remark was addresed to an Ambassador at Peking, who was naterally annoyed, and the relations of:a certain European Power with China were in consequence not of the friendliest nature for sometime after. "You are stupid" is another favourite observation of his Excellency,and that, too, ,Mr. Lo Feng-Luh no doubt finds it expedi- eat to modify.

An extra attraction at the People's Palace Exhi- bition was found on Tuesday in the opening of an East End dog show—a singularly anomalous, title for a canine gathering largely recruited from other quarters of London and many parts of the country. It is only fair to say, however, that certain classes were limited to local exhibits. Among these were many toy dogs, as luxuriantly quartered in cages furnished with " arVcurtains as any of the pee displayed with pride by a section of the Ladies' Kennel Club at West End Shows. llomerton. from anesthetic point of view,is one of the most unin- teresting of the eastern enburba. hut it has a dis- tinction of its own in the dog world. Mr. Barwell's Lill of liornerton and Mrs. Blayney's Kin of Homerton.'a pretty Blenheim. bore off local prizes. and Daisy of Homerton.belonging also to Mrs. Blay- ney,was high in the judges' favour. In the.open classes Mr. 'G. R. Sims' Barney Barnett). who haS made a remarkably successful round of bulldog and other shews, added one more to a long list of honours,and was the object of much attention. A curiosity of the exhibition was Woodlands Alice, a deaf ball-terrier.

div.p: THE FXAMINER, SATURDAY AUGUST 22. 1896

your weakness by -denying your charges. Then, inflamed with passion, you told me that I should never have back my child—never see her face again—until I proved myself worthy to take charge of her. Those were your very words." "I don't deny it," said Lord Champney, "I was mad, Barbara—mad and cruel. If you had only told me as much then as you have told me now, I should have been at your feet. Did I wrong you throughout, Barbara? Did you never love Willard Ames, and was your heart always true to me, even while I doubted you ?" The Lady Barbara drew herself up proudly. "You insult me by such questions," she said, coldly. "Oh, Barbara, Barbara !" cried his lordship, coming a step nearer, and speaking imploringly. "Is it all over between us? If you but knew the misery of the years since we have parted! I have stayed away because I have always doubted your fidelity to me more or less, but my heart has yearned for you all these years! Oh, the long days and the long nights, Barbara! My pride, my anger, my jealousy have kept me from you, but my love at last has conquered all. Take me back, Barbara. Let us begin again at the point when you hard, and cold, and unforgiving, like an insulted queen, and I, stern, jealous, miserable, and cruel, parted by mutual consent. Barbara, my wife, I love you with a love to which my boyish love was weak. Take me back." He held out his arms, as his voice broke down in a hard, dry sob. But the Lady Barbara waved him back. There was a look of pity in her glorious eyes, but a stern smile, awful in its beauty, held its place on her lips. No, Sidney," she answered. " When we parted years ago, we parted for ever. You have the old jealous nature still. You think so humbly of yourself that you would inevitably suspect me of preferring another. Besides, there is a grave between us."

"A grave !" "Yes, a grave. The grave of our little child whose face I never saw. And a piteous look crept into the sternness of the Lady Barbara's face. "You robbed me of my child because of your wicked jealousy, and I never felt the touch of her little clinging hands—l never tasted the joy of seeing my child's eyes look up into mine. She smiled on another woman's bosom. She died in another woman's arms. And my arms, my heart, and my life have been empty." Lord Champney's dark face paled, and his features worked in a convulsive emotion.

" Oh, Barbara 1" he said, is a tone not louder than a whisper. "Hear my defence. You were ill, and near unto death. The doctor said that the child must be sent out to nurse. It was a frail little thing, and he thought it should have country air. We were in London, you know. The doctor knew of and recommended a farmer's wife down in Surrey—a woman with a young child of her own— and our child was sent to her. As Heaven is my witness, I sent her away in love, and meant to bring her back when you should be well enough to take charge of her. Then, as you grew better, I lound those letters, and the demon of jealousy within me was unchained. I told you that you should never have back the child until you swore to me that you were tit to guide her. Oh, I was mad, Barbara; yet, if you had yielded to me in wifely forbearance, all these years of misery might have been spared us. Our quarrel deepened into estrangement. We agreed to part amicably, and thenceforth be to each other as strangers. I went out from your presence a broken-hearted man; yet, even in my bitterest anger and jealousy, Barbara, I must have vaguely felt your innocence, for I went from you to the Surrey farm, intending to send our child back to you." He paused, and searched in vain that proud and passionate face for some token of relent- ing. "Go on ! " said the Lady Barbara. "The woman and her husband were but sub- tenants of the farm," said Lady Chamney, in a broken voice. "I had paid them frequent visits, and they seemed contented and prosperous. But when I went to them, after our separation, I found that they had vanished. The farmer had com- mitted a forgery, and had fled with his family. I inquired of the neighbours, and found that our child had died and had been buried on the very eve of their flight, and no notification of its death had been soot to me. I had the little body taken up and removed to our family vault, and I sent you word. of the child's death. Then, the last link being broken between us, I went abroad. Barbara, If I have sinned, I have also suffered. Can you not forgive me? Oh, Barbara, the sight of you revives my old love, with a million times its old force 1 I cannot live without you ! "
"I forgive you, Sidney," said the Lady Barbara, lowly. Lord Champney's face became transfigured with an absolute radiance.

"Oh, Barbara I" he breathed, coming nearer. "I forgive you Sidney," said his wife, retreat- ing as he advanced, "but I cannot take you back. We must continue to be as strangers. I can never forget that little lonely grave—never! When you can give me back my lost child—when you can place upon my breast the little head that has nestled there only in my dreams—then, and only then, can we be to each other what we were. You see how impossible it is to take up the old life where we dropped it. If I seem harsh and cruel, it is you who have made me so. It is you who have frozen my life at its fountain." The radiant look faded from Lord Cbampney's face, and a haggard and despairing expression stared from his dark eyes. A silence fell between them—the silence of a ter- rible anguish and despair. The summer winds, fresh from the sea, lifted the lace curtains of the open window, and brought on its wings the burden of gay voices and merry laughter from the croquet players on the lawn.

That sound, seeming like a mockery, lashed Lord Charnpney's soul to a bitter fury. "You can have gay company," he sneered, "while my heart is breaking.' "You have lived without me seventeen years," said his wife coldly, "and I daress.y you can live without rue to the end. My young cousin, Ada Gower, lives with me, and my guests are invited to keep her company for a few weeks. lam at times but a dull companion for a young girl. And now," she added. "are we to consider our inter- view at an end ?"
Lord Champney's lips quivered as with a sudden spasm. He staggereu to the window, gasping as if for air.

The old love—the yearning tenderness, the pas- sionate affection he had felt for his wife in the old days—had come back at the sight of her, as he had said, with a thousand times its olden force. His anger and jealousy were all forgotten. I Ne smothered love of years had burst through its bo ids, and was become again a consuming flame. He leaned against the window-sash, wishing that he might die then and there. And suddenly through his anguish and misery a gay laugh floated, piercing his heart like a knife. He started, put back the curtain and looked out upon the lawn.

-His wild eyes scanned every member of the gay group in turn, settling upon the tall and slender figure of a gentleman who stood, with folded arms, a little apart from the others, yet whose face, bright with laughter, showed that he shared in the general gaiety of the group.

The countenance of this gentleman was fair, delicate and effeminate: yet, even from the window, it might have been seen that his bright blue eyes were lit by a courageous soul, and that his effemi- nate face belied his noble, manly and determined spirit. The sight of that fair face was like the sting of is serpent to Lord Champney. "Willard Ames!" he ejaculated. "Impossible 7"

"Why impossible?" asked the Lady Barbara, her face changing slightly with a sudden indignation. "Mr. Ames is my friend, and the suitor of my cousin—" "Ah, yes, I understand!" cried Lord Champney, with a bitter sneer. "I see through your arts, madam. You send me from you—you goad me to desperation—you harrow my soul with reproaches —and all that you may enjoy the visits of your old lover, under cover of his pretended affection for your doll-faced cousin. Fool that I was, I was completely deceived ! So-o INo wonder you are in haste for my departure 1" "I am in haste for it, Lord Champney 1" said the Lady Barbara. "Be kind enough to relieve me of your presence at once!' Lord Champney turned upon her with flaming eyes. "Madam," he said to her, with a desperate cool- ness, "we were never divorced. We were never legally separated. Our private agreement to separate has no legal value, in the eyes of the law you are as much my wife as on the day we were married. I shall remain at Saltair just so long as that popinjay out there remains ! I shall stay here to protect my name and yours. You may order me_a_ room to be I,;ut ready. lam not going away."

div.head: SUNDERED HEARTS;
div.p: THE SUNDERED HEARTS;
OR, A WAR OF THE HOUSEHOLD.
By the Author of "The Double Life," "The &Linn Scheme," &c., &c.
CHAPTER 1. AFTER MANY YEARS.

On the coast of Norfolk, in En-glaind, between nappiabargh and Weyburne, is situated the Saltair Manor, the dower property and the residence of the Lady Barbara Champney. Its wide water front is protected against the encroachments of the sea by a range of low cliffs, and on other sides the estate stretches away to embrace in its wide grasp sunny fields and pastures, woods, parks and all the natural features appropriate to a great and prosperous domain. The house, situated in the midst of a large and sunny lawn, is a picturesque, turreted, stone dwelling, with great bay-windows projecting upon the terraces, and with a high tower which commands a magnificent view of the North Sea. One morning in June, 1869, a gay group of young people of both sexes was gathered on the lawn between the house and the sea. A game of croquet was in full progress, and the little party, numbering seven persons, three of them young girls in picturesque short costumes, the remaining four of the sterner sex, were fully absorbed in the play, their laughter ringing out like silver chimes. In the great bay-window of the drawing-room the Lady Barbara Champney stood, idly looking out upon the bright scene, and upon the glittering waters that lay beyond, dotted with the white sails of commerce and of fishing craft. The Lady Barbara was a royally beautiful woman of some five and thirty years, yet she looked nearly ten years younger. She was tall and queenly, with bronze-gold hair waving back from her brows, and dressed after the prevailing fashion; with a pale and creamy complexion, and with proud, dark eyes, whose glances were as cold as the beams of a winter sun. Her red lips wore an habitual proud curve, and her rare Saxon face, bright with a dazzling loveliness, was strangely haughty and reserved in its expression. "How happy they all are !" she thought, Iler glances fingering upon the group of croquet players. "This is their time for dreaming! I pray Heaven tbat they may never wake up to life's bitterness, as I have done I' •

She moved away, as if the sight of the bright faces and the sound of the gay voices annoyed her, and took up from the table a London paper of the day preceding. Looking over the columns idly, her gaze fell upon the brief list of arrivals in town. _ _
Prominent among these was the arrival of Lord Champney, late minister to an important German court. _

The Lady Barbara started at sight of that name, and her pale face grew paler, and she walked restlessly to and fro the room, soon halting again at the window, a great agitation convulsing alike her soul and her features. .

_ "Back again in England ! " she murmured, her long white fingers twining themselves nervously together. " Back again, after all these years? Why has he come? To torture me ?" She uttered a low moan, and wrung her hands yet more fiercely. At this juncture her roving gaze, wild and rest- less with a great anguish, marked the opening of the great brazen lodge-gates. Again she started, a sudden foreboding seeming to seize upon her. The next instant a horseman rode into the grounds, and galloped up the avenue. 'lt is he I' she murmured, her pallor deepen- ing to ghastliness. "Oh, my God! She drew back hastily behind the flimsy curtains of lace, and peered out at the approach- ing horseman, seeming to devour him with her eyes. "It is he !" she repeated, trembling convulsively, and clinging to the window-sash as a sudden weak- ness overpowered her. "How little he has changed! Oh, Sidney! Sidney 1" She bowed her head, and a gust of sobs shook her frame. The horseman galloped nearer and nearer, the sound of his approach soon reaching her ears. _ _
Then, as if endowed with a sudden strength and energy, she aroused herself, drew her form erect and banished from her face every trace of emotion.
Still listening, however, he heard the new-comer alight at the porch, and give his horse into the charge of a servant, and then heard a quick tread on the marble floor of the entrance hall.
The Lady Barbara crossed the floor to a distant seat, and had scarcely settled the ample draperies of her white morning robe, when the door opened, and a servant announced the new-corner:

"Lord Champney 1" The Lady Barbara arose to greet her visitor, her face as cold and impassive as the face of a statue. The visitor came forward with some eagerness, and halted within a few paces of her. He was a tall, noble-looking man, of about forty years' dark almost to swarthiness, with eyes as black as midnight, just now lit with strange emotion and eagerness. His mouth was trembling under the shade of the heavy black moustache that drooped over it, and his manner was full of a great agitation. "Barbara. 1" he said, holding out his hand. "Barbara is it thus we meet at last ?" The Lady Barbara trembled. His passionate voice, broken with emotion, stirred her soul to its depths. Yet her voice was clear and cold, her manner full of haughty surprise, as she answered: "Yes, it is thus we meet, Lord Champney. And It is a strange meeting, is it not, fora husband and wife who have not looked upon each other's face for seventeen years ?" Lord Champney retreated two or three paces, and regarded her-in silence. "To what may I attribute the honour of this visit?" inquired the Lady Barbara, with icy cour- tesy. "We parted nearly seventeen years ago, by mutual consent, and agreed that our marriage should henceforth be a marriage but in name. To spare me ignominy, and your name the faintest shadow of disgrace, and very ,possibly because you had not sufficient grounds for a divorce," she added, with bitter emphasis, "we agreed that the world should never know of our domestic troubles. We have smiled, like the Spartan lad, while the fox gnawed at our very hearts. But our secret has been well kept. The world does not dream of our incompatibility—is not that the word? You went abroad as ambassador. I came to Saltair, where I have since lived in retirement. The world—the fashionable world, I mean—has been charitable enough to believe me an invalid, and to eulogize your noble self-sacritice in devoting yourself to the interests of your country. I see, however, that you have resigned your post abroad. How is the farce to be kept up now? flow are we still to hoodwink society?" Lord Champney drew a heavy sigh. " Still unforgiving, Barbara he exclaime,, in a passionate voice. "You never loved me." The Lady Barbara's lip curled. "You do well to say that," she said. "I did love you, Sidney. I loved you as wives seldom love. And what was may reward? Your passionate, jealous nature made me miserable from the first. YYou oudsuisscp:vceted redt_neinofowliviantig,4o,atlyierls betterntloia yt_n thou. know at Willard Ames had been a suitor for my hand before yourself, and that I had refused him. From the moment of that discovery you were on the watch lest my heart should turn to Willard—" "Because he was handsomer and gayer than 1," interrupted Lord Chanipney. humbly, " lie was fascinating and bright, and full ot those ways that women like, while I was dark and reserved and stern."

"You had no right to doubt your wife I" said the Lady Barbara. " I gave you a conclusive proof. that I preferred you to all other men when I married you. When our child was born you forgot for a while your suspicions and jealousy—at least, while I continued ill. You thought I would die, and the doctor ordered that the baby should be sentout to nurse. It was sent away while I was delirious with fever. As I grew better you were again the devoted and tender lover. But before I grew entirely well before my child had been brought back to me you found among my trinkets a packet of letters from Willard Ames, one of them of recent data, and full of protestations of love. Willard Ames was incapable of writing such letters to a married woman. Where the letters originated I never knew, but they were forged by some enemy who knew of your peculiar weakness." "You never told me before that they were forged," said Lord Champney, with agitation. " You refused to satisfy my doubts— "I repeat that you had no right to have any doubts of your wife !" said the Lady Barbara, firmly. "Your doubts were an insult to an horkourable_ woraan„ and I would not pander to

The Lady Barbara made no remonstrance. he knew well that to do so would be but to feed the flames of her husband's jealously. Quietly touching a hell, she ortlered a room to be got ready for Lord Cilanipuey, inoicatirig an apartment at some distance from her own. " I shall proceed to make myself comfortable," observed his lordship, with savage bitterness, when the servant had withdrawn. "As you have your guests—your party of sympathizers—it is but fair that I should have mine. It is not safe to trust one's self in an enemy's country alone. I shall send for my luggage immediately, and telegraph up to town to my cousin to follow me here by the first train. Of course you remember my cousin, Felix Warner, whom you used to call a 'self- seeking hypocrite,' and who had spent all these years abroad with me. He came to England three months :is advance of me. • You can proceed with your little drama. Felix and I will be spectators of it—or actors in it, as circumstances indicate."
With a bow of intense mockery, he went out :rwn. her presence.
CHAPTER 11. THE OLD SQUIRE'S DARLING.

In the pleasant and fertile Weald of Sussex, as the district between the South Downs and the Hills of Surrey has been called from time imme- morial, and not many miles distant from the town of Horsham, is another country home, to which we would now call the attention of the reader.

It has not the splendour and elegance, nor has it the extent, of the Sahair Manor. It is, however, one of those sunny English homes which are the boast of the country, and which find so many reproductions in every land to which the English have emigrated. It is called Chessom Grange. The house, built of red brick, is ample in its dimensions, is ornamented with a profusion of elaborate chimney stacks, which are a hospitable feature, and has immensely wide windows, set with plate glass. Upon the east side of the house is a beautiful flower-garden, in front is a lawn, to the westward a charming grove, and to the rear are the kitchen-garden, the offices and the paddocks. Upon the same bright June morning upon which occurred the interview described in the preceding chapter, two persons were sauntering down the short, wide sweep that led from the ambitious porch to the open gates. The elder of the two was Squire Chessom. He was a short, stout man, with a red face and an apoplectic look, evidently an advocate of generous living. He had a genial countenance, bright with intelligence, and beaming w,th an irrepressible jollity. He was, in brief, a kind-hearted, jovial, and rather choleric old gentleman, with a generous purse for the needy, and a generous heart for the sorrowful and the erring. He was equipped for a ride, and led by the bridle his favourite thoroughbred, whom he intended to mount at the gate. His companion was a young girl, who was endowed with bright beauty, as piquant as it was rare. Her complexion was dark, but clear and tranparent, her scarlet lips contrasting with the clear dark paleness of her broad brows and of her cheeks. Her eyes, brown almost to blackness, were velvety in their softness, starry in their splendour, and as changeful in hue and expression as an April sky. Her jetty hair, cut short, clung to her little, well. shaped head iu tiny, close-curling rings. She had the archness, the purity, the sweetness of an unspoiled child, yet in her eyes was the tender gravity of the woman. It's rather warm for you, papa, to ride over to Horsham on the mere chance of getting a letter from Edmund," she observed, tying a tiny button- hole bouquet with a blade of grass. "Why don't you send one of the servants ?"

"Because I've promised to meet a man at Horsham on business. This is market-day, you know, and I am to get my pay for the sheep sold to the London dealer. But what do women know about business ?" asked the squire, with a fond emile. "Give me the posies, Dora, and I'll be off." "As if there was any need for such haste, papa !" exclaimed Dora, with a laugh, as she affixed her bouquet to his coat. "There! That looks nice. You wouldn't be in such haste to go, if you only knew how I miss you when you are gone.' "Then you do think something of your old father, Dora ?" Dora's eyes answered him.
_ A sudden moisture dimmed the squire's eyes, and he laid an unsteady hand caressingly on the girl's bright young head. "I wish Edmund was here!" he murmured. .__

"But why ?" questioned Dora. "It's a great deal pleasanter when he's away, papa. He's so sober and cross, and all he cares for is to make money. I must say so, if he is my brother. Thank fortune, he and I are not alike. See what a little Pharisee I am, papa," she added, looking up at him with laughing eyes. "But it is true that we have no resemblance to each other, physically, mentally, or morally. We might as well have been children of different parents." The squire's mouth twitched a little. A shadow of trouble appeared in his honest eyes. "People who are dissimilar are generally the best of friends," he said. " People like their opposites. About Edmund, Dora." And the squire forced a smile, under which lay hidden a deep anxiety. "He isn't—ah—he is, perhaps, now, the sort of man you'd like fcr a husband. Eh, Dora ? " The young girl made a comical grimace, as if she had tasted something bitter. "Our Edmund the style of man I should like in a husband ? " she exclaimed. "Oh, dear papa, what taste you have! Edmund should have a prim, dignified wife, all back bone, you know—one of the proper, stiff-necked sort of women who never by any chance do an impulsive thing. And as for me, why—"
She paused, her gaze drooping, her sparkling face suddenly flushirg. - - -

The squire noticed that tell-tale blush. He was looking at her keenly, with many anxieties hidden under his this mantle of gayety and badinage. "And as for you, Dora," he asked, taking up her words, "you prefer a town gallant—an elegant fine-mannered gentleman, like this Mr. Felix Warner, who comes to the Grange so often ? " Dora hung her head, but that very act was sufficient answer. "But, Dora," said the squire, "this Warner is no fitting mate for you. I would never have invited him here if I had suspected he would win your heart. In the first place, he is too old for you." "Oh, papa, he is only thirty-five, and I am ^seventeen. Besides, he don't look as old as he ia." "Hair dye, my child !” said the squire, sententi- ously. "You are very venerable, lam willing to grant that," and he smiled; "but there is too much disparity between your age and his. Let the young wed the young, and grow old together. In the second place, Dora, there is too much disparity between your positions."

- - "But how so, papa? If he is a gentleman, lam a lady. Where will you find better blood than that of the Chessoms ?" asked Dora, proudly. "There is not a more honourable family in the kingdom." The squire's lips trembled a little, and a look that was strangely compassionate crept into his eyes. Dora marked the look, but failed to comprehend it. "Well, papa ?" she questioned. "Well, darling," returned the squire, with an assumed cheerfulness. "I am but a simple country squire. Mr. Warner belongs to the younger branch of a titled family. He is the cousin of Lord Champney, the minister to a German court, and he will be the next Lord Champney, if the present lord, who is childless, has no son. Warner told me this himself, and said that his prospects were good for becoming the ninth Baron Champney. I do not believe Warner would make a little country girl, however good and pretty, his wife and an heiress to all the honours he expects to gain." "But what do empty honours amount to, papa ?" demanded Dora. "It is the qualities of the mind and heart that make sensible people's happiness. I am sure that Mr. Warner is better than you think."

The squire looked troubled. "Do you like this man, Dora ?" he asked. l" Yes, papa," whispered Dora, blushing. "I must see him the next time he comes," said the squire, thoughtfully. "I have something to say to him. That is, I must know what be wants. If he is not in earnest, he must go away, Dora. I don't quite like him. He is too oily, too insinuating. I prefer an honest Mildness to his velvety smooth- ness. Is your happiness dependent on him ?"

"Oh, no !" cried Dora. "No, indeed. My happiness isn't dependent on any man, except you, papa. I like Mr. Warner, but I suppose I could learn to unlike him, if necessary." " And you don't love young Squire Weir ?" "Not at all, papa. Young Squire Weir? Why, I don't bez.ieve he ever thought of marrying me. I have know him all my life.' The squire sighed. His thoughts went back to his own private anxieties.
" You-will never marry Warner, Dora," he said. T.d.o not think he will ever stand a test I shall

apply to Min. Are you sure mar yart are so averse to Edmund? How would you like him as a lover? He is a little parsimonious, I grant— a little harsh and cold—but he is honourable, just, and upright." Dora interrupted the squire, crying: "Why, papa, you are speaking of nay own brother. What can you mean?" The squire started, laughing nervously. "You failed to quite catch my meaning, Dora," he said. "I meant a young man like Edmund. He is—a type, you know." "Are you anxious to be rid of me ?" asked Dora, in her straightforward manners and with a glance of mock reproach. "Now, papa, you'd better let match-making alone. I am sure I am in no hurry to leave you and the dear old Grange. If Edmund is the type of the young man you want me to marry, you will have to resign yourself to disappoint- ment, I fear," and she laughed gaily; "for you won't find a young man like Edmund Chessom in four counties. And I'm sure I sha'n't grieve if you can't. I would prefer a less perfect sort of man. Edmund has always regarded me as an usurper, if I am his sister." "Don't, Dora," said the squire, as if pained. "I don't like that word in connection with you. Edmund never could have felt that way. He is too just. Did I tell you I had written to him to come home on a visit ?"
Dora replied in the negative. "Well, I have," said the squire. "I haven't been very well lately. I don't like this dizziness I am getting so subject to. and—"

He checked himself abruptly, as Dora began to look frightened. "There, there !" he said soothingly, patting her face with his horny hand. "I'm an old goose, dear. The doctor 'll put me all right, no doubt. I'll go and see him while I'm in town. Shall I bring you any ribbons or anything?" "No, papa. But about this dizziness?" said Dora, gravely. "You are sure that it is nothing serious ?"

" Of course," replied the squire hastily, looking away from the girl. "What should it amount to? Am I not as hale and hearty as ever? I don't look consumptive, do I? But to return to our subject : I expect this letter from Edmund, which I hope to receive to-day, will ap- point the date of his coining." The squire's manner deceived Dora. Dismissing her fears in regard to his health, she said, gayly : "I'm afraid our rising young barrister can't stay with us very long, and I suppose you want him for a month at the very least. How sober you look, papa. Are you troubled about anything?" "I was just thinking, Dora, that I have some- thing to tell you when I get home. I meant to tell you before this, but have kept putting it off," said the squire, with a sort of desperation. "It is time you knew it. If anything were to

lie broke off abruptly, drew the girl to him, kissing her, and then, with another nervous laugh, led his horse to a stone mounting-step near, and took his place in the saddle. Dora followed him, and laid her white hand on the horse's mane. Her eyes, full of a sweet serious- ness, scanned his face.
"What /AI it, papa . she asked, with wave tenderness.

"Nothing to alarm you, darling. Don't look so sober. We'll have a good long talk when I get back. You'd better take a walk while I'm gone, and don's be anxious. Everything is right." He gently laid her hand off the horse, and drawing his rein tighter, moved away down the road.
At a little distance he halted and looked back.
Dora stood in the gate-way, looking after him wistfully, a shadow obscuring the brightness of her face.

"Poor little girl !" muttered the squire, under his breath. " What will become of her when I am gone? I must not put off making my will another day. After I see the doctor I'll go on to the lawyer's. Poor, poor little Dora He waved his hand to her is seeming gayety, and then rode on, brushing his hand across his eyes and swallowing a sob. Dora stood there in the shade of an acacia-tree until the squire had vanished out of sight, and for some time longer, idly twisting the ribbons of her sun-hat, and musing on his strange words and actions.

"I never knew papa to have an attack of low spirits before," said she to herself. "And yet I cannot think there is anything serious the matter with him. He never looked healthier. What can it be that he wishes to tell me ?"

She became deeply thoughtful, but was aroused at length by the bound of rapidly approaching foot- steps. Looking up hastily, she beheld a small, ragged urchin, with (lusty bare feet and a brimless hat, whose face she had often seen at the hamlet not more than a mile distant.
This urchin, who was panting heavily, having hurried on his way, came up to her and took oil his hat, saying. " Bean't you Miss Chessom ?"
Dora repried in the affirmative.

"Then -'ere 's a note for yer ! " said the boy, ex- tricating a slip of paper from his packet. "Woman over at the 'Are and 'Ounds, Miss, give me tuppence for fetching it. Any answer?" Dora took the note without hesitation. She was In the habit of receiving so many applications for help from poor people that she was not at all sur- prised at receiving the present missive. She opened the note and scanned its contents. They were brief but startling, running as follows:

"To Miss Dons CHESSO/41,—Years ago poverty and deep trouble compelled a mother to give away her child to stringers. For years she never looked on its face, never heard its voice. But when she began to grow feeble, and her other children died one by one, and she was all alone in the world, her heart went back to her first-born, the one who had been brought up as the child of strangers. Dora, do you not understand me? Has nature never whispered to you that you are not of Squire Ches. Born's blood? You are that child! And I—l am that poor mother! Say nothing to the squire— but come to me I Let me look upon your face, if but for one minute. You will find me at the way- side inn, the Hare and Hounds. Ask for Jaw. NABS." Dora read these words again and again, a deathly faintness creeping over her. Not Squire Chessom's child! The words danced before her eyes. An iron hand seemed grasping at her heart. A strange blur shut out from her the sunlight and the landscape. "Any answer ?" asked the ragged urchin. Dora shook her head and waved him away. Startled at her pallor and her stupor, he moved off in the direction he had come. Dora crumbled the note fiercely in her little hand. _ _ _

"It is not true !" she muttered. "It cannot be true! I know better. Papa not my father! The woman should be arrested! She cannot impose upon me!" She fought with a strange feeling for a brief space, and then she said: "I will go to this woman. I can at least see her. There is some mistake in this, or she is an impostor and should be punished !" She tied on her hat and moved slowly down the road, a grey pallor settling down on her face, and a heavy and terrible foreboding settling down upon her heart. What if, after all, the letter should be true

To-day as I pen these lines, one picture from the long' vanished 'oast rises in my memory as clearly as ough it hung on a wall before my very eyes. It is Of a 51/ about fourteen years old, propped up in a great arta' chair with pillows and bedclothes, and gazing through window. He is just convalescing after a long Oa dangerous illness, and is still thin, pale and weak. The strong arms of his loving father have taken him fr°ll/ the bed and placed him snugly by the window in order that he may see his playmates at their games in tb6 th snow ; for the time is mid-winter. They wave their hands to him and he waves his hand feebly to tbell3' The scene is from my own boyhood, forty years ali°' What magic has conjured it up now ? Only a sentena from a letter.

This : " I was so weak that for years I had to t." 3 carried upstairs to bed." A lady speaks thus of her girlhood. What a pitiable thing. It is not what nature meant ; bit alas ! too often what really happens in tlii° perverted world. Children should never suffer Pa' for pain is punishment. For whose offences then—suril not their own—do the little ones sicken and die by' counted millions ?

" From childhood," so runs the letter, " I was alwals delicate. When fourteen years old I got a chill on tbe lungs which left me in a weak state. Indeed, I `4lll always tired and weary, and never knew what it 0/1 to feel strong."

Now, tell me, if you can, what sadder reading one i 5 apt to come upon than this? Fancy a young girl beilig always tired, weary, and weak !—tco weak to climb tbe stairs to her own bed ! so feeole and lifeless as to re' quire to,be carried over the house through which 5136, should have skipped and danced like a fawn. What OL' so crushed her ? Disease? What disease and 1304 caused ?

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DBAR NBLLIN, New gowns are a luxury which many of us can only indulge in once or twice during the season, but hats and bonnets may be varied frequently, and at very small expense, provided one is clever enough to renovate and retrim them at home, and very often the slightest alteration is sufficient to bring headgear up to date. Hats for the demi-saison show a distinct tendency to decrease in size, and with glowing summer on the wane, they no longer resemble huge parterres of flowers. Roses are always great favourites during the first three- quarters of the year, but as the autumn comes round poppies come to the fore, and at the present time they are lovely, especially the real poppy-red silk ones, with their velvety buds, mingled with green or yellow corn, while on very dainty hats and bonnets the double silk Japanese poppies, with pretty crumpled petals in exquisite shad of pale pink or heliotrope, are smart and effective.

A very pretty gardien hat in natural straw is lined with cream lace, and has a beefeater crown, raised at the back, and surrounded by a wreath of roses, or poppies and foliage, with a bow of white ribbon on the top. A bonnet for a comely matron of say 35 and upwards is of fancy green satin straw, trimmed with green satin ribbon, clusters of cherries and leaves, a broad wired ornament of cream horsehair, sewn with irridescent sequins at the back, and smart irrideseent aigrette. The strings are of very narrow green ribbon velvet. A very pretty costume can be made in fancy printed sateen, the skirt being full, wide and gored, and with a smart blouse bodice back and front, the sleeves and the skirt are lined, and the collet and cuff are finished off with pretty lace, and the front box-pleat with three large cut-steel buttons. The blouse draws up at the waist to fit the figure, and a folded band and bow finishes off the waist.

A becoming use can be made in the new silver lawn, with bands of open applique work, show mauve satin. Turn-over collar, a satin neckband, and the waistband of the same. Another pretty blouse bodice with lace yoke back and front, and a high collar covered with lace. This is finished with cut steel buttons, waistband and bow at back, and is lined. A suitable gown for wear during the holidays and the autumn is of :lark blue cheviot serge, the skirt slashed in front with fawn cloth, and adorned with groups of tiny gold buttons and long gold loops. The well-fitting bodice has touches of fawn inserted in a similiar manner, and the three groups of buttons and loops form a stylish and novel trim- ming. The low-crowned sailor hat is one of the latest shapes, and is trimmed with cream ribbon. A serviceable coat and skirt costume is made of heather-brown tweed, the coat made with reversible fronts that may be worn either open or closed. The fronts are lined with light tan cloth, and are buttoned back when the coat is worn open, forming smart light revers. The favourite hue of serge at the seaside and and other pleasure resorts is of a cream colour, and none other is so cool-looking, dainty, and generally becoming. The skirts were all plain, or, more properly speaking, fiat, since some were braided. One dress in cream serge had the coat turned back with a robbed collars and revers, faced with gold braid and gold buttons, and showing a vest of ivory silk muslin, crossed with deep gold-hued satin knotted right in the centre.

div.head: TH E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 22, 1896
div.p: TH E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 22, 1896
"WOMEN'S CHAT."

At the personal suggestion of her Majesty, Mr. J. Manning. the superintendendent of the royal mews at Windsor Castle, is about to retire on a substantial pen- sion,after havii.g served the Queen for no less than 52 yeais. He entered the mews as a stable boy and rose step by step to the highest post of all. Mr. Manning is much esteemed by the children and grandchildren of the Queen. In his earlier years he arranged the riding lessons of her Majesty's family,and the little princes and princesses frequently resort to him for reminiscences of the childhood of their own parents. The recent celebration of the birthday of the Duchess of Buccleuch brings to mind the fact that,notwithstand- ing her Majesty's long reign, our Sovereign has only had ten Mistresses of the Robes, viz., two Duchesses of Buscleuch, two Duchesses of Sutherland, the Dowager Duchess of Atholl, the Dowager Duchess of Bedford, Elizabeth, Duchess of Wellington, the Duchess of Rox- burgh, the Duchess of Argyle, first wife of the present Duke,and for a very short time the Duchess of Man- chester, now Duchess of Devonshire. The Duchess of Beccleuch is a daughter of the first Duke of Abercorn and married in 1859 Lord Dalkeith, now Duke of Buc- cleuch. My readers will remember tbat the Duke and Duchess lost their eldest son,Lord Dalkeith, by a tragic accident while he was out'shooting, some years ago. Homburg is now very full of visitors, and Dr. Yorke Davies has arrived there to look after a smart clientele who are anxious te lose weight. This most fashionable watering place is acquiring considerable repute in cases of obesity, but it is more than probable that Homburg would net be Homburg without its distinguished visitor, the Prince of Wales. The majority of the arrivals boast a "machine," and as the roads are in splendid condition cycling promises to be as much in vogue during the Homburg season as it was in London. By the way, it has now been decided in a county court, that a bicycle ' does not come under the head of "passengers' luggage," and that the railway companies are not bound to send it on by the same train as the passenger! It cannot be thought that such a decision is unreasonable however, although there is no doubt it will make a considerable difference to the plans of cyclists who like to take a railway journey prior to a run on their own wheels. That the steady increase of suicide in Europe has not left this country untouched, may steadily be seen from the return for 1892 to 1895, during which period the yearly numbers have increased from 2,472 to 2,764. A disturbing feature in the case too, is that the increase is uninterrupted, it appears to be following some definite law, and not to be at all dependent upon sudden waves of public excitement, and natural distress. One great comfort, however, is that the increase in these Isles of ours is happily not so marked as in France, Italy, and many other European countries. A well-known French scientist is of opinion that a large number of nervous complaints from which girls of the present day safer, are to be attributed to playing the piano. According to this authority, statistics show that of 1,000 girls who study the instrument before the age of 12, no less than 600 suffer from this class of dis- orders, while of those who do not begin till later, there are only some 200 per 1,000, and only 100 per I,COO among those who never tried to play the piano at all. The scientist believes the violin to be greatly injurious, and suggests that children should not be permitted to study either instrument before the age of sixteen at least. The great man is doubtless right, in so far that exces- sive study in any form is bad, very bad for young peo- ple, but it is difficult to understand that a moderate amount of practice on the piano or violin could upset any but the most delicate child's nerves. Personal experience has taught me, so far, that it is the nerves of the folks destined to listen to the daily practice, that are likely to suffer. Beside all this,sixteen would be too late for any girl to commence her study on either the piano or violin if she hc ped ever to become a really good performer. Apropos of statistics. M. Paul Raymond finds that the consumption of alcohol in Paris actually costs that city the sum of nearly two million francs annually. Taking the number of habitual drunkards to be found yearly in the thirteen " consulting hospitals" which Paris con- tame, and only taking account of those who are in a hopeless condition,he finds that each hospital receives on an average 62 of these unfortunates a month ,nearly half of them being women. This means that 10,000 inhabi- tants are rendered useless citizens every year by alcohol, ' and that instead of earning money themselves they have to be kept at the expense of the nation. Although the shoemakers of to-day bring science and commonsense to their aid, there are very few supporters of the rational boot, that is, one cut to the natural shape of the human foot, with a due regard to anatomical principles, giving ample room for the play of the muscles ; and even at the present moment there are women sill? enough to make their way to Scotland, Switzerland and elsewhere, bent on climbing in high- heeled boots and pointed toes! I would strongly advise those of my sex whose aim and cbject is to enjoy their holidays, to indudge in boots and shoes that fit them, and moreover those with elastic waists—a term applied to the middle of the sole beneath the bend of the foot. They permit the wearer to walk much longer distances than those cut on less hygienic principles. Children should always wear straight soles, straight from toe to heel. As time goes on, it is of the utmost importance that we should carefully notice the position, dictated to us by fashion, for our headgear. A year or two ago hats were worn as far back as possible on the head, with the result that those boasting brims presented a halo-like appearance that was distinctly ludicrous. There are still some mistaken individuals who persist in the mode, and this utterly spoils the best built headgear imagin- able. Our hats, to be quite correct, must tilt forward, and they are to be less trimmed at the back this autumn than formerly. The sides and front are to receive more attention. I notice that many skirts, for autumn wear, built of heavy material, are without lining. This is a mistake, and I would warn my readers to avoid these particular skirts, if they value health, and comfort.—All heavy materials have a tendency to cling, and this is very fatiguine and distressing to the wearers in walking. A thin lining of silkette (a mixture of silk and cotton) does away with this difficulty, and despite all some dress- makers say, scarcely adds to the weight. For coats, Italian cloth is the most satisfactory lining. It is ever- lasting wear and slips on easily over rough fabrics. The fronts can easily be faced with silk, and so give the coat a luxurious appearance. Speaking of "silkette," now diminutives are all very well in their way, but in certain connections their em- ployment Is more disputable. We can put up with "flannelette," "stockinette," " silkette," " leaderette," 'and " sermonette," but we cannot help marvelling where we are to stop when we observe a clerical individual describing himself in the columns of a weekly journal as the "Author of the Churchette." Does he preach from a pulpitette, and address edifying discoursicles to his faithful fiockling, I wonder? Pillows are damaging to beauty, according to Queen Nathlie of Servia—lying upon one, night after night 'ltem the lines of the neck so the Queen says and she ascribes the superb carriage of her head mainly to her avoidance of pillows, and to sleeping on a hard straight bed. Her children are all forbidden to use pillows, and daily have to practice the Eastern custom of carrying a pitcher of water on their heads. There is no doubt that many of us would do well to follow Queen Natalie's ex- ample, both in the matter of hard beds and no pillows, and the pitcher of water form of procedure. STUFFED VEGETABLE MARROW.—Pare and cut in two a good sized vegetable marrow. Scrape out the seeds,rub inside and out with salt, let it drain an hour, then fill up the halves with onions previously boiled a little, and chopped with some sage. Add a little butter, pepper and salt, close up the halves and tie them together with tape. Well grease a dish, and bake in a moderately hot oven. Serve with good brown gravy poured over. " MADGE."

div.head: SHOCKING NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT
div.p: SHOCKING NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT
WA RRINGTON.

On Friday morning at the Warrington Borough Court before Aldermen Harrison and Wright, Councillors Pier- point and ttoberts,and Mr. S. Wright, John Fiddler and Sarah Fiddler, 118 .?ierpoint-street, were charged with neglecting three of their children on the 10th August and divers dates during the past six montas.—lnspector McAteer said the two defendants ,a ere parents of six children. The three children they were charged with neglecting were Alice aged 7,Annie 4,and May 8 months. In consequence of a complaint made to him he (the in- spector), in company with Detective Foster went to the residence of defendants on the 10th inst. He found Mrs. Fiddler under the influence of drink and when they got in she used filthy language to them. She refused to let them see any of the children. Alice ran out and the second child went under the table. He examined this child. There wad nothing in the house but a table and one broken cbair. Mrs. Fiddler and her son refused to let them go upstairs to see tbe rooms. He remonstrated with her for a long time but she would not give in and they left the house. She then came out with a knife in her hand and her conduct in the street was disgraceful. He (the inspector) had repeatedly warned her during the last two years. She was a drunken woman and neglected her children grossly. They were in a filthy condition. Her husband gave her 21s. a week, and she only purchased groceries on the Saturday to last till Monday. Toe house was visited again on Thursday night, and the children were in bed. Ono was completely naked. The male defendant was a sattir respectable man and not to blame.—Detective Foster corroborated the Inspector's statement.—P.C. Corbett stated that,he lived about 200yds.from the female defend- ant. She was often disorderly and many respectable people complained about her. Her husband was a sober, steady man. The children ran about half dressed.—The Chief Constable said the female defendant had been before the Bench four times before.—The magistrates sent her to gaol for one month with hard labour and dismissed John Fiddler.

William Hopwood and Catherine Hopwood,ll, Dakin's Yard, were charged • with neglecting their children, William, Joseph, Peter, Mary and Ellen, all under 16 years of age, on the 11th July.—lnspector McAteer, pro. scouted, and said the defendants were the parents of seven children and they were charged with neglecting five of them. On the 30th of July, himself and Sergeant Chantler visited the defendants' house and found the female defendant and her children in the back kitchen. 1 he children: were insufficiently clothed and very filthy He examined each and found them dirty. One boy aged 10, was dressed iu a pair of pants, all rags, and a portion of a shirt with no sleeves, and almost alive with vermin. The other children were similarly clothed and dirty. The baby, four four months old, was in a corner of the kitchen with its clothes saturated with filth. Mrs. Hopwood said she could not help it as her husband was only earning a few shillings. He told the woman he would let her off if she made some improvement in the home. He saw the bed- ' room and found it very inadequately furnished. He (the Inspector) visited the house on other occasions and there was no improvernent.—The male defendant said he worked 14 hours a day for 12s. a week as a fustian cutter.—The magistrates sail they would give defendants a chance and adjourned the case for a month. James Stockton, widower, of Twelve Houses, was charged with neglecting three children on the Bth August.—lnspector McAteer stated the circumstances of this case which showed that defendant worked in the day and lad to leave the children in the care of his daughter, who also worked.--The magistrates adjoarned this case also, for one mouth.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

DESTROYING GAMV.—At Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Henry Cartwright, 16, a res- pectable looking youth, was charged with having tres- passed on the fields of Mr. Kelsall, farmer, Penketh, in the unlawful search of game, on the 13th inst.—Mr. Browne appeared for Mr. Kelsall, and stated that the offence was a most impudent one, and Mr. Kelsall, who had a farm at Penketla had repeatedly warned this young man to keep off the ground. He had also been warned by P.C. Thorley. On the day in question Mr. Kelsall's son was in the field and saw a quantity of par- tridges drop. Defendant came up and was walking on the footpath with a gun. Defendant asked Mr. Kelsall, jun., and two men named Glover and Scott, who were with him, if they bad seen any partridges " get up." He went back across Mr. Kelsall's field, when be shot a hare. Mr. Kelsall picked it up and asked him why he had shot it. He replied that "he didn't know ;he thought it was a rabbit."—Mr. Browne asked for a sub- stantial penalty to be inflicted to stop defendant con- travening the law.—Mr. Kelsall, jun., said he was the son of Mr. Thomas Kelsall, farmer, Penketh, and on the above date was in company with Scott and Glover in his father's field when he saw a group of partridges drop. He saw the defendant and told him he had no right to shoot there. He also saw him .shoot the hare. —William Glover and William Scott gave corroborative evidence.—lt was stated that the defendant had a license for his gun, but no game license.—The magis- trates said he was also offending against the High way Act for shooting within forty yards of the highway. They characterised the offence as an impudent one, and fined him 103. and costs.

div.head: LARGEST MUSIC SCHOOL) IN TH WORLD.
div.p: THE LARGEST MUSIC SCHOOL) IN TH WORLD.

In the August Number of the "Windsor Magazine." F. Kllckmann gives some glimpses of the Guildhall School of Music. " When one nears the building itself there is no occasion to read the brass plate to learn that it is London's largest music school ; that fact announces it- self vigorously through all the windows in the place— and they are many. The impressions reeeived outside are decidedly intensified when one enters the building. Wherever one goes,along corridors or up the broad stone stairease,a babel of musical sounds pervades the whole atmosphere. Scales in different keys are being harrassed from countless violins. A familiar Beethoven sonata seems a new and unknown work when heard in conjunc- tion with a Chopin polonaise, both being played with firm and vigorous touch on grand pianos in adjacent rooms. As one ascends higher and higher in the building an orchestral class, containing perhaps a hundred per- formers, adds its quota to the general din; the booming vibrations of the organ pedal-pipes give a feeling of solid basis to everything, while above it all ' there runs a loud perpetual wail as of souls in pain,' though this is occasioned by nothing more serious than innumerable singing professors imparting instruction to innumerable diligent pupils. Yet much has been done to tone down this cacophonous state of affairs. Each class-room has not only double windows but double doors, and every effort was made when the school was being built to render the walls as noise-proof as possible. Hence it is merely the onlooker who is in any way disturbed by this troublous sea of sound ; each class-room bears nothing but its own per- formance. The general scheme of instruction provides that each student should remain in a class-room while two other lessons are given, in addition to the one he or she receives. Another rule is that no one, not even a parent or guardian, shall be permitted in the room while lessons are being given. There is no occasion for the semblance oi a chaperon for even the youngest of the lady students. Mrs. Grandy is amply appeased by the presence of the various others who it about the room taking their prescribed amount of onlooking. It is interesting to go over the school and watch the professors at werk. This can be done without in the slightest degree interrupting them, as all the upper halves of the doors are of glass, and the occupants of every room are open to the scrutiny of the passer-by. Curious pantomimes these lessons will often appear when one can only see the gesticulations of the teacher . but hear nt thing that he is saying."

div.head: LI HUNG CHANG.
div.p: LI HUNG CHANG.
VISIT TO MR. GLADSTONE.

Li Hung Chang broke his journey north on Saturday in order to pay a visit to Mr. Gladstone at Hawarden. The Envoy drove from Chester, and on arriving at the Castle was very cordially greeted by Mr. Gladstone. A private interview lasting for three-quarters of an hour took place, in which Li Hung Chang complimented Mr. Gladstone on his great services to his country and engaged him in discussion on general politics. The Envoy, in acknowledging the naval supremacy of Eng- land, remarked that her colonial possessions and her wide commercial interests necessarily required this sup- eriority at sea, an observation which led Mr. Gladstone to say that our colonies were united by perfect good feeling. Li Bung Chang expressed the conviction that an extension of the railways and the development of the resources of China would undoubtedly lead to an increase of the wealth and comfort of the country. Before ldav- leg Li Hung Chang inscribed his autograph in several books and received a gift of several volumes from Mr. Gladstone. After a stay of an hour and a half at Hawarden the Chinese Envoy proceeded by special train from Chester to Barrow-in-Furmess.
II AND MR. GLADSTONE'S WEALTH.-CATECHIS- ING A RAILWAY OFFICIAL.

It will be remesnbered that on Saturday afternoon, when the special train conveying Li Hung Chang and his suite reached,Chester General Railway Station,it was run into a bay siding near the Queen Hotel, where it re- mained some time before his Excellency was carried in a basket chair to the carriage waiting to convey him to Hawarden Castle on a visit to Mr. Gladstone. The reason then assigned for the Viceroy not immediately alighting from the railway carriage at Chester was that he was indulging in sleep; but what has transpired since has proved the Viceroy was not asleep, but, on the con- trary,very much awake concerning certain matters. In , order to prevent the crowd of spectators encroaching too near the compartment in which his Excellency was seated Mr. Reddish, the station ;superintendent, placed a num- ber of officials, including Relief Stationmaster Brereton, within a short distance from the carriage. Observing Mr. Brereton, in the uniform of the London and North- Western Railway Company., his Excellency directed his native interpreter, Lo Fen Luh, to request his presence in the compartment. bin Brereton immediately com- plied with the request, and the interview extending about twenty minutes, was of an inquisitorial character, the questions being sometimes almost mirth-provoking. His Excellency opened the conversation by asking what was Mr. Brereton's age, and Mr. Brereton, who is a young man, replied ; and the distinguished foreigner quickly asked if he were married. Receiving a negative reply, Mr. Brereton was asked why he was not married. A somewhat evasive answer was given, and then his Excellency questioned him as to his employment, whether he had been promoted, how long he had been in service, and the amount of wages he was receiving. The Viceroy then asked Mr. Brereton if Mr. Gladstone was an old and infirm gentleman and what was his age. Mr. Brereton said he believed Mr. Gladstone's age was eighty-five, and that he was not infirmiThe next interrogations were as to the distance of Hawarden Castle from Chester, and whether Mr. Gladstone had any daughters at home at the pre- sent time. Mr. Brereton replied that Hawarden was about seven miles from Chester, and Miss Helen Glad- stone was staying at the Castle. His Excellency's fol- lowing question was "Is Miss Gladstone married ? " and being informed that she was not he asked 's Why?" but Mr. Brereton was unable to give any information upon that point. The Viceroy appeared concerned respecting Mr. Gladstone'e social position, and inquired if he were popular. not particularly so in his own neighbourhood, but in tbe country generally. Mr. Brereton said he judged that the venerable statesman was exceedingly popular in the Hawarden district, and in other parts of the country, judging by the number of visitors uho journeyed to Hawarden to see him and hear him speak. Li Hung Chang remarked "Then he keeps an open house," to which Mr. Brereton answered affirmatively. "Is Mr. Gladstone wealthy, and has he a large estate?" was the succeeding question. Mr. Breret on said he did not think Mr. Gladstone possessed very great wealth, but he did not seem to " hanker" after wealth, being apparently contented with his possessions. Mr. Glad- stone's home was surrounded by a large estate. These answers were evidently interesting to Li Hung Chang, for he instantly put a further question to the effect that if Mr. Gladstone was not very wealthy why did not the people of the country subscribe to improve his pecuniary position. This was, however, a matter cn which Mr. Brereton could offer no explanation. The conversation then turned !on railway metals, and his Excellency said that the day previous he had been in conversation with Lord Tweedmouth, who asserted that the London and North-Western Railway Company had 1,000 miles of lines. "Was that so ? Is Lord Tweed- mouth a director of the company ? " asked his Excel- lency. Mr. Brereton said he knew Lord Tweedmouth was one of the principal directors of the company, and that it was quite correct the company possessed 1,000 miles of railway. Being asked if he knew whether Mr. Gladstone was a`director or a shareholder of the com- pany, Mr. Brereton said he was not sufficiently ac- quainted thereon, but it was possible Mr. Gladstone was a shareholder. "Are you a shareholder ? " followed, and Mr. Brerston smilingly replied that he was not ;and in answer to the query why he was not one, he said he had not the means to invest. The remainder of the questions dealt with the weight of the metal per yard, &e., and Mr. Brereton after answering to the best of his ability, was thanked by his Excellency for the informa- tion, and his unique experience ofi being catechised by China's greatest statesman concluded. The Viceroy,after being carried in the basket chair to the carriage, pre- sented the railway porters with one gold twenty franc piece,valued at 15s. Bd.
OXFORD LOCAL EXAMINATIONS.
SUCCESSFUL WARRINGTOS STUDENTS.

The Division Lists in the Oxford Local Examinations were issued on Monday morning by the Secretary of the Delegacy. Compared with last year there was an Increase of no fewer than 1.258 candidates examined,the total being 7,314 (3,596 boys and 3.718 girls), viz , 2,141 preliminary, 3,626 juniors, and 1,547 seniors. Of these, 1,505 preliminary, 2,642 juniors, and 1,165 seniors passed, making a total of 5,312, against 3,959 last year, when the number examined was 6,056. The premier position in the First Class of the Seniors is gained by T. K Johnston, Boston Grammar School (principal. Mr. W. White), and the second place is secured by H. W. Middletor, Royal Grammar Sohool, Sheffield (principal, the Rev. E. senior). Amongst the Juniors, in the First Class, C. H. Windridge, King Edward's School, Aston (principal, Mr. E. W. Floyd), is placed first; and F. G. M. Stratton, King Edward's School, Five Ways, Birmingham (principal, the Rev. E. F. M. MacCarthy), second. Of the pre- liminary candidates in the first class F. Burdett, High School, Wakefield (principal, Miss McCroben), is first ; and L. W. Grensted, Merchant Taylors' School, Crosby (principal, the Rev. Canon Armour), second. The silver Tindal offered by the Royal Geographical Society to senior candidates is not awarded, but for the bronze medal J. A. H. Watson, Merchant Taylors' School, Crosby, and W. V. Sidaway, Dudley Grammar School, are equal. The Cobden Club prize is carried off by Miss L. A. Barrows, Church College, Edgbasten. The fol- lowing junior candidates are recommended for the silver medals offered by the Royal Geographical Society :—A. J. Smith, Liverpool College. Shaw-st. ; and M. E. Bridge, St. Monica's Convent, Skipton. For the first time exhi- bitions were offered to the boy and girl candidates placed respectively highest in the honours list. Amongst the seniors T. K. Johnston, Boston Grammar School,and Miss E. Studwick, Queen Elizabeth's School, West Kensington, are successful; 'and the exhibitions for juniors fall to C. H. Windridge, King Edward's School, Aston, and Miss E. M. Walker, High School, Nottingham. In several towns the University extension lectures have been used in the preparation of pupils in certain specific subjects, and these have proved a distinct ad- vantage. That the University is in touch ith the edu- cation of the mintry is indicated by the large increase in the number of candidates, and the delegates have shown every readiness to adopt suggestions made to them by experienced heads of schools. PADGATE. THE RIXTON POLICEMAN.—P.C. Ryder, who has been stationed at Rixton for the past two years, has been transferred to Bury,dnd the vacancy at Rixton has. been filled by P.C. Clarke, who commenced his duties on Monday. TRIP TO HAWARDEN.-011 Saturday the members of the select classes (male and female) of the Wesleyan Sunday School had a trip to Hawarden, accompanied by a few friends. They left Bank Quay Station by train at two o'clock for Chestar, where a 'bus was in waiting to take them to Hawarden. The weather was delightfully fine, and the drive proved mose exhilarating,the scenery through:which they passed being charming. Hawarden Castle was visited, together with the park, where some time was spent, the party finding much to interest. Whilst in the park the exaursionists had a good view of his Excelleth:y Li Hung Chang and his suite. The party also saw Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone. An excellent tea was partakers of at the Glynn Arms Hotel, atter which the j return ournry was shortly commenced. Warrington was reached a little before ten p.m. THE POLICE AND POACHERS.—WhiIst a police sergeant and three constables were returning at an early hour the other morninc, from land belonging to Mr. James Newton, farmer,where they had been watching in the hope of securing the person or persons who had lately been doing considerable damage to Mr. Newton's pro- duce, they noticed when near Paddington Locks, three men, evidently poachers, coming along the Cheshire side ,of the river Mersey towards the locks, carrying some- thing rather bulky. The police concealed themselves, and watched the men carefully stow their possessions in- to a large hole. On the constables making their appear- ance, the men at once ran away, leaving what they had hidden in a hole. On a search being made the hole was found to contain bags with 18 rabbits in them, and also three large nets. These were taken away by the police, and have neen confiscated and since sold, the proceedi going to swell the county fund,

div.head: BRITISH RULE IN ASHANTI.
div.p: BRITISH RULE IN ASHANTI.

The "Mission World" publishes a translation of an account given in the" Allgemeine Missions-Zeitschrift " by the Rev. Mr. Ramseyer, missionary of the Basel Society, of the change effected in Ashanti as the result of British rule. The following are some extracts from the article :—" In Ashanti there has been such an upturning of things as I had never dreamt of. Coomassie is, in fact, a picture of what has taken place all over Ashanti. As one that dreams, I stand in the street. Where there was formerly a whole complex system of houses and I streets, everything is cleared away, and a number of labourers are busy taking out the roots of the fetish trees that have been cut down, under which so many poor creatures were slaughtered. The place of skulls, hard by the market-place, is cleared. Only a beautiful row of trees remain. But at the foot of them there atill lie (although, as the officers tell me, there has been the burning of human bones going on for many days) great heaps of human bones. Oh, the awful cruelty ! And yet there are voices raised to declare that it was wrong to go against the Ashantis. Only a look at these heaps of skulls would surely silence such foolish murmurers. This morning we went into the villiage Duro, in the neighbourhood of which were once placed our huts. That delighted the people, Here is that European ISiisse. Come. Same is here.' And the people were so glad when I told them that the mission- aries would now remain in Coomassie, and that now had come the time of peace. They told us that the whole country rejoiced at the arrival of the English. Every- one had wished it, but no one could have dared to say so. The Governor was, as I have said, most friendly, and he told us some of his experiences on the journey from the coast. He passed through Mampong, Nsuta, and Agona. In one town, where he remained overnight, he had military music played, and he noticed that a woman could not restrain herself from singing and danc- ing before the band. He sent secretly to inquire what she was singing, and learned that every strophe ended with the words, 'No knife more, no knife more.' The Governor had, in all the larger towns, the execationer's knife brought to him, and declared as he took the knives that the taking over of the country by Europeans meant the stopping of all human sacrifices and other atrocities. . . In fact the Governnient of Ashanti is now at an end. This morning we were in Bantama, which is the mausoleum of the kings, and where such numbers of poor creatures were slaughtered. The mausoleum itself has been burned. In the ruins one can discern, to some extent, the cells where the skeletons of the kings were preserved, and where there was daily the cooking of food—professedly for them. On the other side of the road stood the remains of the tree where :the victims- -12 to 15 at a time—waited the signal in front of the mausoleum for their being beheaded. This happened regularly twice in the year and often at other times as well, as at any festival of the town. Now this is all over! God be thanked. The Governor has, with celerity and vigour swept it all away."

div.p: THE American presidential cosi- The American . continues to exci Contest. te a vast ametilit .4Aci of interest not only in the 1.3411•7 a States but in this country as well. It has been Olt that the present election will be more impor,tlll2,a in its consequences than any that has taken p v since AnnARAm LINCOLN waS returned on the 011 of the great Civil War.- In some respects the CO ditions that at present prevail in the ITO States are similar to those of thirty-five a thil4ll six years ago. As a rule presidential contests 111'1 I been conducted on party lines and both the get parties, Republican and Democratic, have be!,,,re pretty fully represented in each State of t'Pf Union. On the present. occasion the line ° cleavage between the 6upporters of the two candi° dates appear i to The not so much political territoiial, just as 'it was priori to the el, War. In 1860 it :was North against SontP; now it is East against ,West and South. •Western States have been rapidly developed te: ing the-last quarter of a century and they are P 0 ginning to assert a very powerful influence in th politics ofithe Republic. A bone of content' has been found iu the currency question. leg EasternEStates, or at least the predominant class in those States, are practically solid in their or port of tlie.,existia,g gold standard, while the agrre culturistecf:the•West , and South appear t° 11, equally' determined to introduce a bi-metallic cu'; rencyiftlieyscan capture;the government of tb, country: Mr. Melinnkv, the Republican 13°°, inee, is, therefore, in this co&est the represeu: tive of the mono-metallists of the East, and To; BRYAN, the "boy orator of Nebraska," as t- Democratic candidate, has, been styled, will ch".o pion the'catise.,of the bi-raetallists of the 'W and woolly West." To some people it may sler that the mere* , question as to whct 'gold alone or gold and -silver conibio% should be regarded as standard currenbco/ is too academic and abstruse in its nature t° 11 tl'e the subject of a -bitter cohtest. But after a . interests involved are :of a very plain and praotitcl3o character—in fact`as plain and practical asiot borrowing and lending of money. The 01)%00 bankers and financiers of the East are the W(3° of money and the productive classes of the jo and South are the borrowers. The questieu dispute between these two powerful secti00:110 the community is really as to the interest oat should be paid on these loans. It might se°Eacooro this is a dispute that should be settled in a of law rather than by a heated political c t it paign, but the Western farmer does not 100 k in that way. He points out that he obtaned .„a le.au,. to, develop his
