Stead he could pay the interest upon that loan with the price of—lot us say—one hundred bushels of wheat, but that now owing to the fall in the price of wheat, or in other words tile decreased value of wheat as compared wit gold, it takes something like two hundred bushels to pay the interest that becomes due every year. This, of course, means ruin in the case of a wheat grower whose holding is heavily mortgaged, and it was said by one speaker at the Democratic Con- gress that everything in the Western States i s ortgaged, from a farm to a sewing machine. The Western farmer has another argument by which he assures himself of the justice of his cause. When told that the fall of prices is due to natural causes which are beyond the control of governtoents he disputes the assertion and points to the fact that until some years ago the American cur- rency was hi-metallic, that is to say debts, no ioatter of what amount, could be paid either 10 gold or silver, sixteen parts of the latter coin being reckoned as equal to one part of gold. That hi-metallic currency, he contends, was abol- ished at the instigation and through the influence of the powerful financiers of the East, and, rightly Or wrongly, he maintains that the ruinuous de- cline in the price of agricultural produce corn- tneneed with the degradation of silver from the Position of a standard metal. On the same ground he argues that the restoration of silver as a standard metal would bring him and his class to something like the old position when he could trleet the payments on his loan with the price of a hundred bushels of wheat. It will be seen, there- fore, that it is not merely what might be described aa a " debating society" question that is exciting the intense feeling that is now being generated in the United States. The Western farmers are ghting just as much for their own solid interests as were the Southern planters In the days of slavery, and, indeed, so are the financiers of the Eastern States. The presidential contest tuts also a solid financial interest for the people of this country, and especially for that sec- tion of them who have investments in the United States. As a matter of fact the English "gold bugs" are held up to as much if not more oppro- brium in the speeches of the Democrats as the gold bugs," of New York, and if the currency of the States is depreciated by means of bi-metallism nglish investors will be as heavily hit as the American investors themselves. They would still tie doubt receive the same number of dollars—or What is equivalent to dollars—in return for these investments, but these dollars would not have the Purchasing power that they have at the present time. Hence the very pronounced hostility to Mr. tayAN which is shown by many influential Eng- lish journals and especially those of London, and the approval which they bestow upon Mr. 4cl(irary in spite of his "high protection." The Presidential contest will be decided at the begin- ning of November and it may be taken for granted that the progress of the struggle will be watched With the keenest interest.

LORD SALISBURY was installed as Lord Salisbury. Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports on Saturday, and he made a sPeech on foreign affairs and national defence Which has caused a considerable amount of specu- lation during the present week. His reference to the Turkish troubles were in the nature of another warning to the Sultan. The state of the Otto- tun Empire he describes as a gaugrene which Inay at any time threaten the "health and Security" of the whole of Europe. At the same time he declines to volunteer to undertake the role of the physician and to perform the necessary surgical operation in regard to the Sultan's dis- turbed dorniniollS. e, however, reminds the other Europaan powers that the danger has already been allowed to exist for too long :a period, and that it may at any time lead to a " dis- turbed equilibrium in the European atmosphere." Lord SALISBURY is clearly of opinion that tile time has not come for any abatement the preparations for defeiice in this country. He ventures upon the rather curious Prediction that the next naval battles will take Place in the "narrow seas," in other wprda, we euppose, the English Channel. This porti on of the PREMIER'S speech has naturally been much Commented upon in the French newspapers, as it 18 taken to imply that the next fighting at sea Will take place between English and French ships. It is very doubtful, however, whether Lord SALIS- BURY had any such idea in his mind. He proba- bly thought that an allusion to the " narrow- seas" was an appropriate one to make when Speaking as the Warden of the Cinque Ports. On the question of general armaments Lord SALIS- BURY was certainly very emphatic. In his Opinion the time for exertion has not passed by, and still less has tha time for preparation. He , hopes that when the danger does come our pre- parations for it may be adequate to the require- ments, The speech on the whole was rather curi- ously worded, and it is not surprising that it should at the present time excite a good deal of comment.

The librarian's report for the year, read to the Free Library Committee, shows that during the year 777 borrowers tickets have been issued, mak- ing an increase of 75 on the previous year. At the Present time there are 8036 books in the library and the committee no doubt with a desire to keep the leading department up to date, has purchased 155 e w works during the year. No town now-a-days eomplete,without its public library and Runcorn may fairly claim to be a possessor of a libraiy equal to the demands of its population.

Another successful year's work has been com- pleted by the Runcorn School Board and the reports ,Rent in by H.M. inspectors speak highly of the efficient manner in which the schools are taught. The bone of contention now between the Educa- tional "pow ers that be" and the local School Board is that some of the school buildings do not afford adequate accommodation for the scholars, arid in two instances the Inspectors speak :very f-trollgly on the subject. At the same time the Board itself is desirous of doing everything possi- ble to make its system efficient, and no doubt in time the alterations desired by the Department will be effected. Meanwhile the members of the School Board,together with the teaching staff, may be con- gratulated on the uniform and eminently satisfac- tory reports that have been obtained. The resigna- tion of Dr. McDougall from the Board came as a _-hurprisP to the meeting on Tuesday. Regret was pressed by the members,as Dr. McDougall has for "IL long time been a punctual and painstaking mem- ker ot the body.

The common tramp as a rule is an undeserving object of sympathy so that Guardians in dealing with him should not be in- influenced by sentimental considerations. Care should be taken, however, to entrust a responsible official, with powers of discrimination, in dealing with the real vagrant and the bona fide seekers after employment.

Signs of the flying summer and the rapid ap- proach of autumn may be seen in the approach of the Rugby football season. At Runcorn the cup- holders are making every arrangement to ensure a successful season and this week the members of the club have been sojourning at the Isle of Man on the subscriptions raised in celebration of the suc- cess of the clitis in the cup competition. This year's competition in the Lancashire section carries one back to the days of the West Lancashire Challenge Cup as the rules governing the competition are much the same though the laws of the game are somewhat altered. The ties will be played off on the "knock-out" system, and Runcorn will meet nearly the same team as participated in the cup fights in the old days. The Northern Union this year is "the Union," and the clubs in it have a capi- tal list of engagements for the season.

Winter is signalled also by the renewed activity of the Technical Instruction Committee. These classes re now part and parcel of the educational system cf the town, and the stuuents will probably look forward with interest to the seasons prospec- tus which is in course of preparation. The ques- tion of subjects is in the hands of a capable sub- committee the members of which will, no doubt, base their decision upon the support extended to last year's classes.
RUNCORN AND wiDNES,

SUCCESS or A RUNCORN STUDENT. Mr. W. H. Wiswall, of Runcorn, has, obtained a first class in the advanced stage of steam at the recent ex- amination in connection with the Liverpool School of Science, Technology and Art. CAMDEN WESLEYAN CHOIR TRIP.

The members of this choir accompanied by several friends drove to Cnester on Wednesday. That city was reached about noon, and after dinner the party sailed up the Dee to Ecclestin Ferry. A very pleasant day was spent. HOLY TRINITY SCHOOL RUNCORN.

The scholars attending this school decided to go to Frodsham for their annual treat which took place on Wednesday. On arriving at the hills the children took part in the games arranged and tea was served by the teachers. The Rev. Dr. Preston and a number ef friends accompanied the party. THE CASTNER-KRLNER CHEMICAL WORKS RUNCORN. Residents in Runcorn and district will hear with plea- sure that the directors of the above company have decided to make their works at Weston Point double the size originally decided upon. The completion of the works is rapidly being carried forward and operations will likely enough be commenced before Christmas.

div.head: RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB.

The Wednesday section of the above club should have gone to Altrincham but a change wa4 made, by a un- animous vote of the members at the last minute, in favour of Chester. A fair assembly theretore enjoyed a pleasant run to that quaint city the attractions of which seem never to pall upon Runcorn cyclists. RUNCORN FOOTBALLERS AT THE ISLE OF MAN. It will be remembered that when the football club of Runcorn secured the Lancashire cup a subscription was raised for the purpose of giving the men an outing. The subscription reached Rtl.o and on the strength of the accumulated money the playing members have been to the Isle of Man this week. Everyone knows the capacity of the Runcorn footballers te enjoy themselves and as the Isle of Man is at the height of its short season at the present time it is needless to add that the men have,one and all, had a thoroughly good time.

CLOSING OF THE RUNCORN SHOOTING RANGE. The Inspector of Musketry for the Cheshire district has after an examination decided that the Runcorn range shall not be used until further orders. This action has been taken in consequences of a complaint by the Runcorn Urban District Council,through their secretary, pointing out that the shooting interfered with the games and sports of the young people frequenting the Common. The range has been in use about thirty years and the order to close it will cause some inconvenience to the local corps as the nearest range now is at Hartford. The rifle gold medal ^ompetition is still unfinished and the prize meetim, has not been held so that the closing of the range will materially alter the arrangements for these events.
ALLEGRO Tar OF TALLOW AT RUNCORN.

John Massey, Nelson-street, was charged at the Run- corn Police Court on Thursday morning-with stealing on the 17th inst. one barrel of tallow valued at £2, the pro- perty of the United Alkali Company.—William Holford, weighman at the Company's works, said he last saw the tallow on July 21st but identified it as the property of his firm by the marks on the barrel. He weighed the tallow and marked it so that be knew the mark. Pri- soner used to work for the comp4ny and knew the place very well.—P.C. Gregory stated that he apprehended the prisoner at three o'clock on Wednesday and found the tallow at the back end of Nelson-street with some timber. Prisoner when charged said he knew nothing about it.—The case was remanded until Monday. RUNCORN AND DISTRICT CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY'S ANNUAL
EXCURSION

The excursion organised annually by this society took place on Wednesday when a special train was chartered for Llandudno and Rhyl. The train left Widnes at 6.45 and Runcorn at 7 o'clock and about 400 members ot the society assembled, Runcorn being responsible for more than half of that number.the rest assembling at Widnes, Ditton and Frodsham. The train made an expeditious journey and the two watering places were reached in good time. Once there the excursionists were left to their own devices and an enjoyable time was spent ac- cording to the particular tastes of each member. The weather was very favourable and the pleasure to be found in tiae two watering places was entered into with spirit. Runcorn was reached in good time in the even- ing. Capital arrangements for the comfort of the pas sengers were made by a committee appointed for the purpose and carried out by the railway company.

div.head: DRUNKENNESS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DRUNKENNESS AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday at the Runcorn Police Court before Messrs. Joseph Handley and F. J. Nerman,James Wood- ward was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Greenway-road at one o'clock on Tuesday morning. P.C. Nicholls stated the case and prisoner was fined 2s. ed. and costs or in default seven days. At the same court William Dunstan was fined ss. for being drunk on Monday night. On Wednesday morning before Mr. F.J. Norman and Mr. S. Taylor, C.C., Charles Bell,a seaman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Tues- day and refusing to quit the licensed premises of the Holyhead Harbour Inn. Mrs. Le Coat said that prisoner came into her house in the afternoon drunk,and wanted beer and she refused to serve him. A ship mate asked her to let prisoner lie down and she had the man put to bed. Shortly afterwards he got up again and com- menced to make a disturbance. She asked him to leave the premises and as he refused she called in the police.— P.C. Nicholls stated that he was called to prisoner who was creating a disturbance in the Holyhead Harbour Inn. He refused to leave the house when wilted and witness was obliged to lock him up.---Fined LI. and 6s. Bd. costs. At the same court Ellen Moran an old offender, was sent to gaol for one month for being drunk he previous night.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

PRESENTATION.-00 Wednesday evening a smoking concert took place at the Conservattve Club, Frodsham. The chair was occupied by Col. Ashton, and there was a large attendance. A very interesting feature in connec- tion with the proccechngs was the presentation of a hand- some marble timepiece to Mr. Henry riley, for his valu- able ssrv:ces associated with the establishment oi the club, and as hon. secretary since its opening. The Chairman, in banding the gilt to the recirient, spoke of the energy he had displayed in the eveSe of Conservatism in the Frodsham section of the Erldisbury Division, and his earnest efforts in securing the sneces of the institu- tion in which they were assembled. 41thongh the present was a handsome one he could assure) Mr. Tiley that it did not by any means show their full appreciation of his services. Mr. H. G. Litiaker, Mr. Joseph Gorst, and ethers also here their testimony to the good work done by Mr. Tiley, after which that gentleman said he had always taken a keen interest in the cause of Conser- vatism, and he intended to continue kis efforts. Numer- ous toasts were drunk, and the proceedings were enlivened with songs.

div.head: EXAMINER SATUROAY, AUGUST 22. 1896.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATUROAY, AUGUST 22. 1896.
RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL

The usual fortniahtly meeting was held on Tuasday at the Dutton Workhouse. Present :—Mr. J. Mclntyre (in the chair), Messrs. J. Knowles (vice-chairman), J. Bran- dreth, S. Woodward, T. Baxter, C.C., W. Pickering, C. W. Davenport, J. Darbyshire, H. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams, T. Lewis, W. Bradford, T. Darlington, T. Wright ; J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (assistant clerk), Swinton and Diggle (surveyors), and T. Farrington (nuisance inspector).
THE ISOLATION HOSPITAL QUESTION.

The Lnal Government Board drrw the attention of the Rural District Council to their letter of the 19th September last and to the statements in the last annual report of the medical officer of health to the Rural Council ar to the need of hospital accommodation for the isolation of cases of infectious disease occurring within the district and they inquired how the matter now stood. The Clerk was instructed to state that a committee had been formed to consider the matter.
INTERFERENCE WITIT ROADS.

The Chairman of the Castner Kellner Alkali Company Limited made application to lay 4in. drain pipes along the highroad from the Salt Union Work 4 to the works of the Company at Weston Point. The expenses in con- nection with the same would be paid by his Company, and the road made good to the satisfaction of the Coun- cil. They also desired permission to cross the road from Weston to Weston Point between rumps Brow and farm in the occupation of Mr. John Griffiths, they undertak- ing to keep a man on the road with a flag to protect traffic and to make the road good and to be only used in the day time. Not wanted for longer than two months.
Permission was grante3,subject to the company enter- ing into the usual agreement. This was the whole of the business of public import- ance.
BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO., LIMITED
HALF-YEARLY MEETING.

Sir John T. Brunner, Bart., M.P. (chairman), pre- sided over the 31st half-yearly general meeting of the shareholders of Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, held in the Law Association Rooms, Liverpool, on Thursday afternoon. _ _ .

A motion to adopt the report and balance-sheet for the half-year was submitted by the Chairman, who remarked that the shareholders would notice in the profit and loss account an item of £18,518 17s. 6d., profit on sale of investments. A number of the investments which the company held had advanced greatly in value, and the directors considered that it was not good business to hold them at their existing price. They came to the conclusion that the price of these securi- ties which they held was an inflated price, and they did not consider it good business on behalf of the shareholders to hold them as a company. In the report it would be observed that the directors proposed to place to the reserve fund the sum of £18,658, which was £l4O more than the profit on the sale of investriaLnts. The reason why they proposed to put to the reserve fund an amount slightly ,higher than that shown as the profit on the sale of investments was that they were ex- pecting within a few weeks to receive on account the 7906 preference shares to be issued at £7 premium,which would give an amount of £55,342. If they added to- gether £18,658 and £55,342 they would find that they got e round sum of £74,000 which, if it was added to the £442,000, at which figure the reserve now stood, would give a reserve fend of £516,000. They would have seen at the end of the report that the direc- tors proposed to write off the patents account only £5OO instead of the usual £2500, because they did not like to let it appear to the shareholders that their patents were of so small a valhe as they would appear to be if £2500 were written off. In their opinion these patents were of very much higher value than that at which they stood on the 30th June,namely, £9702. They would notice that the small amount of £127 had been added to the freehold land item in the balance-sheet,and that a much larger amount, namely, £45,984, had been added to the cost of the Alkali Works. That item of additions to the Alkali Works had been spent at Silvertown in the main and at Winningtoa, and at both of those places very largely for the manufacture of caustic soda. Sir John concluded by roving that the report be adopted, and that a dividend of 30 per cent. be declared on the ordin- ary shares of the company, and of 7 per cent. on the preference shares. Mr. Coghill seconded the motion, which was unanim- ously adopt&l. Mr. Jones moved that the directors, oth:_‘r than the managing directors, be paid the sum of £6OO for their services during the half-year. So long as the directors could sing to them the tune of 30 per cent. they would dance and dance with joy. (Laughter and applause.) Dr. Darsie seconded the resolution, which was unani- mously passed. On the motion of Mr. James Handley, seconded by Mr. Irvine, Messrs. T. W. Read and Co., chartered accountants, of Liverpool, were appointed auditors of the company. This concluded the business of the ordinary meeting. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders was afterwards held, Sir John T. Brunner again presid- ing, for the purpose of considering and passing a special resolution carrying out certain alterations in the articles of association. _ .

The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the special resolution, explained that the first alteration was to in- crease the nominal capital of thg company frona two millions to three milliens. The reason for their propos-

ing this was that, after the 7,906 new preference shares were taken up,the two millions would be exhausted. It might seem to some of them a big jump from two to three millions,but it was only a matter of paying a little sooner than might possibly be the case the £1 per thou- sand ituty to the Sta. e. The next alteration was merely formal,and authorised the directors at their discretion to issue shares with or without a premium up to the nom- inal amount of unissued capital. He had no doubt their experience was that whenever capital had been issued the shareholders had been treated with scrupulous fairness, and they might rely upon it that in any fur- ther issue of shares all the share-holders would be treated equally with that fairness which they had experienced hitherto. The last alteration in the articles to which he would call attention was perhaps the most important, and it provided that a balance-sheet should only be issued once a year instead of half-yearly as hitherto. The reason for the change was simply that with the great extension of their business they found that the tax upon their staff of taking stock twice a year was more than ought to be put upon them. Their desire was to take stock only once a year, and to issue a bal- ance sheet and report only once a year as from the 31st March in each year. Mr. Galloway seconded the resolution, which was adopted. In acknowledging a vote of thanks, the Chairman said he had expected that a question would have been asked as to whether shortly there would be a call upon the shares now at £3 10s. paid. They were aware that the alkali trade was in a very depressed condition, wed that being the case great exertions were necessary on the part of the directors to maintain the dividends. It was tetter, therefore, from their point of view not to ask for money which would water the dividend at present, but rather to get money as they were prosperous at the rate of four per cent, by the issue of preference shares. When they saw the prospect of making 30 per. cent out of every £1 that they called for from the shareholders, they might depend upon it that in their interest and in the directors' own in- terest a call would be made, but it was not business to take up money at 30 per cent, at a time when the market prices were so low. (Hear, hear.) The proceedings then terminated.
SHIP CANAL. THE CANADIAN CATTLE TRADE.

In view of the probable development of the cattle trade between Canada and Manchester via the Ship Canal to important dimensions, it is interesting to learn that the whole of the cattle and sheep landed from Mon- treal by the steamer Feliciana were sold within a few hours after they had been certified fit for sale. The prices realised were in every respect satisfactory, and compared more than favourably with those obtained for the same class of animals at Birkenhead. The condition of the animals left littleif anything to be desired, and the fact that only one sheep was lost on passage speaks well for the provision made by the owners of the steamer for the efficient conduct ot. the traffic. There appears to be every desire on the part of the wholesale trade in Manchester to support the direct importation of foreign cattle to this city, proof of which is afforded by the circumstance that most of the leading firms here were amongst the purchasers of the present consign- ment. Some of the beef intended for transportation by rail has been chilled in the room specially equipped for that purpose at the Foreign :Animals' Wharf, Old Trafford, and has also turned out satisfactorily. All that now appears to be wanting to ensure the successful extension of tke trade is a more regular and frequent service of steamers. This is really one of the first essentials in the matter, as both shippers and receivers have insisted on the constant arrival of animals here, if Manchester is to divert the trade trom Birkenhead. One of the main objects of Mr. Marshall Stevens' visit to Canada is to negotiate for such re„ ular lines of steamers from North Atlantic ports as will secure this result. rhe Manchester, Bombay, end General Navigation Company intimate that another steamer of the Furness Line will leave Montreal for Manchester in about three weeks' time, and that in addition to cattle and sheep she will bring a large quantity of Canadian apples,,of which there is an exceptionally heavy crop this season. The Gulf of Genoa is busily discharging frrzen meat and rabbits and other cargo from Australia. The meat is being removed to the Corporation Cold Air Stores, the rabbits are being sent to Liverpool, and the wool by rail and barge to the York- shire manufacturing districts. It is worth noting that in:addition to the articles referred to the Gulf of Siam is discharging 500 tons of ore which was originally in- tended for Glasgow. The Royal Prince proceeded down the canal on her outward passage to the Mediterranean yesterday, taking with her thJ largest cargo yet shipped from Manchester to ttiose ports. The Clan Liner Bul- lionist will be on the berth in the course of the next few days, to load for Bombay. She is one of the new turret deck steamers of (dinner pattern to the Imperialist, which left here for Bombay last month, and was the first of this class seen at Manchester.

MORE GRIEVANCES AT RUNCORN. 1 There are numerous indications that the Ship Canal Company are putting forth earnest exertions to get all possible traffic to Manchester. Several vessels chartered for Ruscern have recently been prevailed upon to proceed onward by the giving of special terms, and the same advantages were offered to a captain this week.but for the present he declined to go further than Runcorn. A Greek strainer Aghios Joannis, containing 2,240t0ns of grain for Messrs. R. Bennett and Co., Manchester, from Marianopol,has been prevented from going beyond Runcorn lay-by in consequence of her steel masts being too high to permit her to pass under Runcorn Bririge. Pressure was nrought to bear upon the owners to cut them, but this they strenuously refused to do under any circums!ances, with the result that after two or three days' detention at Easteam a berth was found for her at the lay-by, where she is now being discharged auto lighters. Numerous complaints are being made by shippers, of workmen belonging te the Bridgewater Undertaking of the Ship Canal being diverted from un- loading sailing vessels in the docks to discharging steamers in the Ship Canal, which they contend will act prejudicially to captains and owners utilising the docks at Runcorn. A list of complaints is being formulated for presentation to the District Council.—" Liverpool Daily Post."

div.head: LUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: LUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
A YEAR'S WORK.

The annual meeting of this committee was held in the Council Chamber, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening •, pre- suit Mr. %V. Handley (in the chair), Messrs. H. J. Grice, W. Hankinson, T. Riley, J. Pritchard, Rev. J. Sirrpson, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, J. D. Jones (secretary and librarian.

The Librarian presented the fourteenth annual report of the committea for the year ended June, 30th, 135'6. The number of borrowers tickers issued during tho year was 777, being an increase of 77 as compared with last year. The library had been opened for the h-;sue of books 241 days,and 22,713 books had been taken out, being an increase of 131 for the year. The daily average of issue was 96. There had been added to the library ,177 volumes during the year, 155 of which were purchased and 22 presented. The total number of volumes in the library was now 3,036. The second course of half-hour talks about books and authors was very successful. The lectures were delivered in the large art morn of the Tech- nical Institute (by the kind permission of the Technical Institute,Committee) and were listened to with great comfort by larger audiences in consequence of the change. The lecturers and subjects were as sollows :- Rev. C de P. Gliddon, "Whittier ": Mr. Joseph Pritchard, " Halton Castle "; Mr. John Skeaping, " Nature Vast "; Mr. James Wilding," Canon Kingsley " ; Rev. J. S. Simpson, "The Wizard of the North " ; Mr. J. J. Ogle (Bootle), " Wordsworth" ; Dr. Bowman, Northwich, " Books, their use and abuse." The reading rooms con- tinue to attract large numbers of readers, and are often overcrowded. The committee again present their thanks to the various donors of money, books, periodicals, and newspapers.-The financial statement showed that the year was commenced with a balance in hand of £7 98.8 d. and the receipts were :-Free Library rate, £193 145.; fines, £8 us. 9d.; borrowers' tickets, £6 15s. 4d.; papers and waste paper sold, £2 143. 9i. ; members' subscrip- Arms, £1 25.; donations, £5 ; small items bringing the total up to £226 193. 11d. The expenditure included, salary of librarian and secretary, £6O ; new books, £54 105. 2d.; magazines and newspapers, £4l se. ; bookbind- ing,£ll 4s. 101; printing and stationary, £l6 135.; rent of library premises, £36 ; fittings, £3 65. 6d.; advertis- rnents,£l 195.; sundries, £2 35. 2d. There was a balance in hand of 3s. 31.-It waa decided to accept the report and to have 150 copi.s printed. The cash statement for the past month shows that the the receipts were £22 35. id., including balance from July of £2l Bs. 10d. Several small items; and 183.10 d. balance due. The expenditure was £23 3s. id., the chief items being salaries £5, new books '.16 143. 7d. The number of books issued was 903, being an increase of 168.

div.head: FIRE AT DUTTON WORKHOUSE.
div.p: FIRE AT DUTTON WORKHOUSE.

A somewhat alarming outbreak of fire took place on Monday evening at the Dutton Workhouse, and had it not been for the prompt action of the officials the safety of the building would have been greatly endangered. The fire was discovered,in the tower where painters have been busy renovating, and it was found to have a strong hold on the structure. Mr. Cunnah immediately had the fire appliances belonging to the house at work and soon a strong jet of water was playing ovi the flames with so much success that the fire was mastered before it had time to do much real damage. The damage that was done however, is covered with insur- ance so that this unwonted expense will not fall on the long suffering ratepayers.

div.head: DISMISSAL OF A CHESHIRE
div.p: THE DISMISSAL OF A CHESHIRE
SCHOOLMASTER.

With the object of obtaining further information as to the School Board agitation at Norley which has been brought about by the dismissal of the master of the Church school, a reported has visited the village. Mr. George Lake, the former schoolmaster, was interviewed and stated that he was obliged to leave the schoolhouse on Monday. He asserted that he knew of no legitimate reason for the dismissal, and he intended to remain in the village until the ratepayers had given their verdict at the poll. He went on to say :"It is very significant that in the spring of 1893 I received a notice from the vicar, against whose interference in school matters I had been bound to protest. The notice at that time was not signed by other managers, and they supported me in an appeal to the Bishop of Chester. An indignation meet- ing was also held in the village, and resolutions protest- ing against the viczr's conduct in dismissing me and closing the school were passed. Then the Bishop came down, and I was reinstated by him. Things have been unpleasant since, and I regard the present position of affairs as the outcome of that old disturbance. I have done nothing wrong ; but, for MY own sake, I could not tolerate the Vicar coming into the school and taking en- tire charge, closing it when be liked and giving holidays without consulting me in any way. I have asked the managers for an explanation of my dismissal. One said they required a certificated mistress in place of my wife, whereupon I said she was quite prepared to resign. Another stated that financial difficulties were the canse. I can get no further explanation."—The reporter then visited the Vicar (the Rev. C. R. Nunn), but beyond the remark that "the managers desire a change, and do not feel called upon to give explanations of a private matter," he declined to make any statement.

-- A correspondent, writes :—There was a lively lieeting of the parishioners on Monday evening, respecting the school and education. The people,rather than lose such an efficient teacher, have made up their minds not to let him leave the p3rish, a school board was decided upon, and on a vote being taken,twenty-five persons assented, whilst se wen dissented, the latter then demanding a poll. It is understc od that the matter is to be laid before Sir J. T. Brunner, and rather than be domineered over by Priestism the people will build a school for themselves. This will practically mean the closing of the church schools as the bulk of the'children belong to Noncon- formist parents.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton on Tuesday, present Mr. J. Knowles (chair- man), the members of the Rural District Council, Revs. Dr. Gastaldi and J. Simpson, Messrs. S. Taylor J.P., C.C., A. R. Norman, S. Marwood, with the Clerk (Mr. J. Ashton), and the Deputy Clerk (Mr. G. Ashton)..

„ GUARDIANS AN'D 'THE OLD AGE PENSIONS. The Sleaford Union submitted a petition adopted by them in relation to H.M. Government providing assist- ance to aged and deserving poor by state aided old age pensions and stated that the Guardians were of a strong opinion that inasmuch as the excessive amount of out- door relief administered within the Lincolnshire Unions, went direct to the aged and deserving poor that the pre- sent system of taxation whereby the agricultural com- munity bore the whole of the taxation with respect of the maintenance of those cases was wrong in principle and unfair to the ratepayers. The petition urged upon the Grovernsnent the necessity of providing assist- ance by the State aided old age pensions from the Imperial Exchequer, so that the aged and deserv- ing poor might be raised above the lot of common paupers, and their support be an equal burden on all classes of the people, and earnestly trusted that the recommendation of the present Royal Commissioners ap- pointed by the Government would be favourable to the formation of some practicable scheme. Mr. Heywood moved, and Mr. Mclntyre seconded a resolution to the effect that the matter be referred to the Parliamentary Committee. The motion was carried. RESIGNATION OF A 'VACCINATION OFFICER. Mr. R. Moore, of 53, Church-st., Runcorn, forwarded his resignation of the position of vaccination officer. The resignation was accepted. TREATMENT OF VAGRANTS, The Local Governmeet Board wrote,stating that their inspector, Mr. Dansey, reported that vagrants relieved at Dutton Workhouse were as a rule only detained one night. The attention of the Guardians was drawn to the Board's circular letter of the 25th February last, on the subject of vagrancy, and they were urged with a view of securing uniformity of treatment from this class of paupers to carry out the regulations with respect te detention contained in the order of December 18th, 1882. Mr. Brandreth : What is the arrangement? The Clerk: Keeping them in two days. Mr. Woodward : Is the house staff sufficient for the purpose. The Chairman : Ido not know 'whether the:staff is sufficient, but I do not think there is sufficient accom- modation. Mr. Brandreth : It is a question of this. If the vagrants are detained two days we shall not have so many coming here. Mr. Woodward : If Mr. Brandreth's statement is right and we keep them for two days it will not be a question of accommodation. (Laughter.) I suppose them two days. we might try it for a time. Mr. Taylor : What effect will it have ? The Master : In some cases it has been good, in some cases the reverse. In Chester they found it did not do to keep them, Mr. Taylor: In what way ? The Master : They had more vagrants. The Chairman : According to the notice we are bound to keep them. Mr. Mclntyre: That is the law. Mr. Brandreth: It is a question as to how they are to be treated. They must not be treated like gentlemen' they must be treated as tramps. Mr. Baxter : I think that was the cause of the failure at Chester. They did not find the vagrants enough work to do. It was decided to try the effect of complying with th Local Government Board's request and the master wae asked to prepare a report showing the effect of it. THE TEA AND SUGAR SUPPLY.
The Visiting Committee recommended that an ounce of tea and four ounces of sugar per week be allowed to 20 female inmates whose names were mentioned.—The minutes were adopted.
FIRE IN THE MOUS&

The minutes of the House Committee contained a reso- lution to the effect that a committee had been appointed to confer with the Insurance Company on the matter of the fire on Monday night. Mr. Stokes in moving the adoption of the minutes, pointed out that the night previous (Monday) the Board had a narrow escape of the house being destroyed by fire, a room in the tower having caught fire. Had it not been for the energy of the master and the use of certain appliances which had recently been provided, he did not think the fire would have been coped with. Consider- able damage was caused to the building. Mr. Darbyshire seconded the adoption of the minutes and they were passed.

div.head: BEER MONEY OR BEER.
div.p: BEER MONEY OR BEER.
The Clerk said he had been asked as to what officials received on allowance for beer. All the officials had the allowance except the two recently appointed—Miss Cunnah and Miss Jones.

Mr.Darbyshire objected to the system of allowing beer money, as he thought it was a silly system. None of the members would make similar stipulations with regard to their own servants. Mr. Heywood asked the clerk whether the teer allow- ances were included in the salaries, and paid by the State,or whether the Local Government Board only sanc- tioned the payment of the salary, the Guardians pay- ing the money for beer. If it was the latter case he would propose that the salaries be all altered, and the money allowed in lieu of beer be added to the salary. The matter was dropped. This concluded the busi- ness of the Board.

div.head: DANGEROUS DRINKING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DANGEROUS DRINKING AT RUNCORN.
IN'TERESTING STATEMENTS AT THE POLICE COURT.

On Thursday at the Runcorn Police Court, Lawrence Cain, a seaman of the ship " Albion " now lying in the docks, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Percival's-lane, Runcorn, at 11.30 on Wednesday night. —P.C. Wylie in proving the case said he found prisoner drunk after:eleven o'clock in Percival's-lane on Wednes- day night. Prisoner was lying down against some" rail- ings" and as he was incapable of taking care of himself, and not.in a state to go to his ship, he (witness) locked the man up for safety. —lnspector Hicks said there had been many sailors drunk lately 2nd they endangered their lives by going back to their boats along the canal or river while in that state. Only a few wceks ago they had two fatal accidents in one week.—Prisoner was fined ss. including costs.

div.head: PLEA OF INSANITY.
div.p: PLEA OF INSANITY.
PRISONER SENT TO GAOL.

On Tuesday morning before Messrs. Robert Garnett, E. J. Guest, and Dr. T. S. Smith, John Henry Hardman, aged 27, was charged with having on the Ist August, fe- loniously embezzled and stolen £l2 4s. 4d. the money of his masters, Messrs. John Poole and Co.—Prisoner who appeared to feel his position, pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable (Mr. L. Talbot), said the circum- stances of the crime were as follows. The prisoner had been for nine weeks prior to Aug. Ist, a servant in the employ of Messrs. Poole and Co., Limited, tea mer- chants, echo bad branch businesses in many towns including Warrington. Prisoner managed the local branch and part of his duties was to collect the money from the customers. On Saturday the Ist August the firm estimated that he should have collected between £l2 and £l3, which was to be handed over to them the following Monday. Instead of doing sr; however he ab- sconded on that day, and it was discovered that he had taken a ticket to uston Station. All trace was then lost, but a watch wae kept an his father's house in St. Helens and he was apprehended some days after the theft. In mitigation he should say that prisoner had told him he had no recollection of anything after a certain hour on the Ist of August. His father had been mentally afflicted at one time of his life and he believed that the same affliction had fallen upon hill. He first came to his senses in Watford near London where he had been arreated as a wandering lunatic and then allowed to go. He came back to St. Helens and was arrested as stated. _ _ _ _ _ _ _

Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins defended the prisoner and said he bad received a letter from prisoner's father, a late well-known Government official, m which he stated that it was true that there had been a mental weakness in the family. Prisoner had told him (Mr. Jenkins) that on Friday, the 318 t of July he went to Seafortb to see the young lady he was engaged to, and then returned. From that point he remembered nothing until he was locked up at Watford for being a wandering lunatic. As that had happened there must be something wrong in his mind. _ .

Mr. Garnett : Is there any proof of his having been locked up at Watford. The Chief Constable : I have written but have not yet received an answer. I believe it, though how he became a wandering lunatic I don't know. Continuing, Mr. Jenkins said that on the Saturday over £l4 came into prisoner's possession from the sales that had taken place, and after paying £3 7s. 6d. to himself and his assistants as wages, he had a balance of £l2 4s 4d.Mr. Jenkins asked the Bench to take into con- sideration the fact that prisoner had borne an irreproach- able character, and also that he had suffered an extra- ordinary and sudden breakdown, such as took place in the characters of even great men. An inquiry was made by the Bench as to what money prisoner had, and the Chief Constable said he had got rid of all the money somehow. Mr. Jenkins : It is not drink. It seems to me an ex- traordinary thing. The Chief Constable: It all went in about 10 days. Mr. Poole, manager for Messrs. Poole and Co., said he was given to understand that prisoner went to Liver- pool on the Thursday, came back, sent his men away, and went away again on Friday. His mind was not so disarranged as to prevent him sending very kgible tele- grams. On Saturday he was also able to go shopping for his own use. Previously he had done his duty well. Witness had checked the accounts every week and found one or two losses which were unaccountable. They did not, however, think Mr. Hardman guilty of that. Prisoner : I'll pay every penny if I get work. I was coming back to give myself up. The Chief Constable; You went a long way round. Prisoner: I only went over Runcorn Bridge to see my father. The Chairman said they had taken everything into consideration and listened to what Mr. Jenkins had so lably put before them and therefore they would only send prisoner to gaol tor two months with hard labour. Prisoner : Thank you, sir.

div.head: FREE TRADE TRIUMPH.
div.p: A FREE TRADE TRIUMPH.

A short time ago we had, says the 1' Manchester Guardian," occasior to notice the satisfactory figures contained in the cabled reports of Mr. Reid's Free Trade Budget in New South Wales. From the mote detailed report sent by the correspondent of the "Times "it now appears that those figures were satisfactory beyond all expectation. The introduation of Mr. Reid's Free Trade policy was abrupt and drastic; for New South Wales, though generally spoken of as a Free Trade colony, bad, it must be remembered, been committed in a period of aberration to a distinctly Protectionist policy. Many,even among Free-traders themselves, prophesied that the inconvenience caused by the sudden shifting in the field of operations for capital which would result from the removal of the tariff would inflict serious in- jury in many industries. They pleaded for a gradual relaxation; but Mr. Reid held his way,and at one sweep introduced his great fiscal change. So far from the prophecies of the alarmists being fulfilled, the "Times" correspondent is able to write : " There is not an interest in the country "that can honestly say it has been injured. The Mort's "Dock Company, which was singled out as an enter- " prise that would have to be shut up, is planning a "new and larger graving dock to take in the largest 1" class of merchant vessels. Never in the history of "Port Jackson wa the steam flee!t so large or so magni- " ficent." It is only fair to admit that Sidney harbour in all circumstances has i the advantage over other i Australian ports, for t s there that vessels come to coal. New South Wales is the Newcastle of Australia. Apart from. that, it is, of course, the Ifree port that attracts shipping, as surely as a candle attracts moths, though with happier results. Save for its passenger triific, the Protectionist Port Phillip of Victoria is almost a el'ad p rt. Again, it was prophesied that the land of the New South Wales would go out of cultivation when the duty was taken off wheat. Mr. Reid acres m tookor eoff wheat, and there are now 200 000 .crop than lila year. Of these 156,000 the underdu t.. acres are growing wheat. Truly Mr. Reid has triumphed all along the line.

div.head: SOME RECORD FAMILIES.
div.p: SOME RECORD FAMILIES.

A correspondent of the "Telegraph " writes as fol lows with reference to Mrs. Hare, of Flarlesden :—" In the Harleian MSS. in the British Museum the extraor- dinary entry has been found concerning a certain weaver in Scotland who had issue by one wife (a Scotch woman) of no fewer than 62. Only four daughters, it appears. lived to be women ; 46 sons, however, at- tained their majority, most of them, we are told, were living at Newcastle-on-Tyne in the year 1670. Note may next be made of an inscription (according to Pennant) on a tomb in Conway Churchyard, " Here lyeth the body of Nicholas [locker of Conway. gentleman, who was the 41st child of his father, Win- locker. by Alice, his wife ; and the father et 27 child ren ; 1637." A perhaps more reliable it of domestic history is that related in connection with the entry Of Charles V. into Ghent as Count of Flanders. At the head of the procession rode Proudiy old Oliver Minian, in front of a troop of 21. What made Oliver ride so very proudly? That loyal troop was composed entirely of his own lawful sons; whose mother, it has to be added, had likewise borne him ten daughters. A local history of Cumberland avers that at Kirton-le-Moor, in 1797, a "man and his wife, accompanied by 30 children might have been seen proceeding to church to the christening of the 31st' ; while a prtition presented to the Duke of Norfolk, as Earl Marshal, in the year 1693, by one Thomas Greedhill, surgeon (author of a work on

'Embalming') st*owetli, • That, in considera' ion of your petitioner being the seventh son and the 39th child of one father and mother, your Grace would be pleased to signalize it by some particular motto and augmentation to his coat of arins, to transmit to posterity so uncom- mon a thing.' The Earl Marshal awarded his petitioner a demi-griffin' and other distinctions. div.head: VIrICULTURE IN SOUTH WALES.
div.p: VIrICULTURE IN SOUTH WALES.

GREAT SUCCESS OF THE MARQUIS OF BUTE. It is not generally known that the Marquis of But 43 is a distinguished viticulturist, who has devoted much patience and capital to the task of proving that it is possible, to grow really good wine within the limits of Great Britain. Twenty-one years have elapsed since lais lordship determined to try the experiment of planting a vineyard in the open air on his South Wales estate. The scheme was a good deal criticised at the time, and pro- phecies of utter failure were indulged in which have not been justified by events. The first part of the vineyard at Castel! Cock was planted in the spring of 1875, but it was not till 1881. that a really good crop was obtained, when the whole of the vintage, with the exception of a hundred cr so bottles for the use of the castle, was sold at 60s. per dozen to a wine merchant at Cardiff ; and some of this same wine, when offered at public auction two years later realised 115s.pur doz-311.1t was described as resembl- ing in flavour and quality a first-class still champagne. In 1887 ten hogheaus were obtained, and by that time Lord Bute was so satisfied with the results of his experi- ment that be p:auted a second vineyard at Swanbridge, a rather more favourable situation, sevea miles from Cardiff. In 1893 enormous crops of grapes were ob- tained both at Castel! Cock and Swanbridge, with the result that forty hogsheads of wino were made,these be- ing sold by the 110ble marquis, under a licence held. in his own name, for an aggregate sum of £3,ooo—that one season's results recouping all the expenses incurred during eighteen years' experiments. It is too early to speak of what the yield this year will be, as the gather- ing of the grapes does not commence till the middle of October.

div.head: SCOTU-INDIAN ROMANCE.
div.p: A SCOTU-INDIAN ROMANCE.

An article in the " Scotsman " recalls an interesting Scoto-Indian romance which is suggested by the an- nouncement that the famous Beguen Suniroo's palace of Sardhana, near Meerut, with all its works of art and grounds surrounding, are for sale. About a century and a half ago an Ayrshire herd-boy named James Macrae lost his lather, and removed to the county town, where, by running messages, he added to the income of his mother, a washerwoman. The lad spent all his leisure about the ships, where he picked up a scanty education. In one of thee he went secretly to sea. For the next 30 years nothing was heard of him, till in 172 e, as Captain Macrae,he was sent by the Madras Government to reform abuses in the East India Company's settlement. Sumatra. So well did he do this and other duties that the washer- woman's son became Governor of Madras, and held that office for five years. After forty years' absence from Scotland, Macrae returned to Ayr with a fortune esti- mated at not less than £lOO,OOO. His mother was dead. His only sister he found to be the wife of a d:ssolute joiner who lived by fiddling at %cddings. Himself an old bachelor, the retired Governer of Madras devoted his fortune to the advancement of their children, his four nieces. One received the estate of Oranzefield and a box of tea so large that the chest ia still proserved,and she married the Sheriff-Clerk of Ayr. The Fecond was tochered with the estate of Alva, and her husband was the Erskine who became a Scottish judge under the title. The fourth married Captain Macrae, who became notorious in Edinburgla as a duellist. But the ex- Governor's interest centered in the third, who, like the Begum Sumroo's representative in England, married a peer. She became Countess of Glencairn, the then dying uncle bestowing on her the barony of Oc:iil- tree, which cost him £25,000, and diamonds to the value el £45,000. Their son it was who befriended the poet Burns, who wrote in his "Lament for James, Earl of Glencairn "

But I'll remember thee, Glencalrn, And a' that thou h3st done for me. The rich Governor presented. Glasgow first with the equestrian statue of King William, and then with £5,000 to meet the fine levied on the citizens by Prince Charles. Roceut investigation into the old records of Madras reveals many facts most honourable to the Ayr- shire adventurer, who thus raised himself to be one of the best governors it ever bad.

THE BANK QIIAT STATION LOAFERS. Os Monday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Court. before:the Mayor, Alderman Harrison, and Mr. F. Monks,Thomas Durkin, Percivars-fold,Patrick Fallon, 2, Rose-yar I, and John Butler, 12, PereivaPs-fold, all labourers, were charged with having on the 6th'August, obstructed Parker-street by standing on the footpath and preventing' persona from passing.—Butler wai the only one to appear and he pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Turner stated that on the day in questiun he was sent specially to Bank Quay Station to look after such men as the defendants and found these three there. They strod for about a quarter of an hour at once upon the foot- path and as soon as passengers came from the station they ran up and forced themselves in front of the passsengers in trying to carry their parcels. Witness watched them for about half-an-hour and he told them he should have to report them. They set him at defi- ance_—A fine of 40s.atd costs or one month's hard labour was imposed upon each defendant.

THURsasx.—Before Mr. S. Chandley (in the chair) and Col. Ridgway. A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER IN THE MARKET.—AIbert Davies described as a printer from Manchester, was charged with frequenting the Market Place with a felonious inteat at 4 o'clock on Wednesday afternoon.—The Chief Constable said that in the course of Wednesday afternoon P.C. Newey was on duty in the market when he saw prisoner acting in a sus- picious manner. He was following groups of women with his hand at one side and his fingers in the position which was euitable for picking pockets. Newsy saw hint try several women's pockets and then thinking that he himself was oloserved he asked Michael John Knight. a county court bail- iff to watch prisoner for a time. Knight did so and in the course of half-an-hour saw him detiberately attempt to pick the pockets of several women. Newsy followed him out of the market and not receiving a satisfactory answer to his questions he locked prisoner up.—Newey and Knight both corroborated ani prisoner made an ingenious defence, which however,betrayed his familiarity with pocket-picking, and he was sent to gaol for one month.—Some minutes after prisoner had been conducted below, Detective Sergeant Monaghan came in'court with a pair of mud-coloured silent shoes, which he had just found in prisoner's lodgings. These suspicious articles were shown to the magistrates who were further convinced of prisoner's felonious intentions. HE FOUND IT BEFORE IT WAS Lo,T.—Richard Lowe of Wakefield-st., was charged with stealing from a coal yard in Dallam-lane on Tuesday evening, a brush head value 10d. ,the property of William Farrington.—The Chief C instable stated lEat Farrington. a coal dealer, went to the yard in question, ail! placed the brush on the buffer of a w•ggon while he loaded his cart. When he had.finished. he missed the brush and made inquiries.—Thonsas Smith. foreman of the yard, heard him, and searched for the brush himself. Some ttirea hours later Smith saw prioner go to a waggon and take the brush from a place of concealment under it. Smith went to him and he said he had just found it and desired Smith to say nothing about it Information was given to the police and prisoner was arrested.—He had been up before for theft and was now sent to gaol for 14 days hard labour.
DRUNK AND DISoRDERLY.—Frances Riley, 20th app ,arance, was fined ss. and costs or 7 days for being drunk and dis- orderly in Turner-st., on Wednesday evening.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Captain Withington (in the chair), Mr. Wm. Boughton. and Mr. John White. RIDING A BICYCLE ON THE FOOTPATH. Thomas BeMeld and John Chimoey were charged with riding bicycles on a footpath in the township of Burtonwood on the 2nd inst., and were each fined Is. and costs.

AN ALLEGF.D FOWL-STEALER AT BURTONWOOD.—John M'Achm, of 54. Fairclough-street. Burtonwood, w4s charged with being found on the premises of Thomas Howard, with intent to steal,and with assaulting Poli?.e-Constable Grundy. Mr. Riley, of St. Helens,defended.—Police Constable Grundy stated that he and Police Constable Bishop stationed them- selves at night on the 9th inst. in the cartshed on Howard's farm to watch for fowl stealers. When there the prisoner came In his stocking feet, waited and listened at the gate. and then jumped over, and listened sgain. Ultimately he stood actually close beside Grundy who collared him by the neck. A struggle began, in the course of which the prisoner shouted for help and struck out at the policeman.--Mr. Riley. in defence, said prisoner was there with no felonious inten- tion ; he had gone there to sleep.—The ms.gistrates bound M'Adam over in the sum of £lO on the first charge, and fined him 10s. and costs on the seeond. Two OFFRNCFS AND TWO PENALTIES.—Wm. Plinston was charged with being druulc while in charge of a horse and cart at Sankey on Tuesday; he was further charged with assault- ing P.O. Thorley at the same time and place.—P.C. Thorley said that ou the night of Tuesday he saw the defendant in Sankey. Me was in charge of a horse and cart and drunk. He fell off the cart. Witness went to him and defendant struck him with a whip. When taking him into custody defendant butted witness in the chest. He had to get the assistance of two Warrington constables to look defendant up. —P.C. Turner and P.C. Whittaker corroborated and defend- ani was fined 108. and costs for the first offence and 10s. and costa for the second offence also.

POICHING AT AsToar.—Joseph Spruce was charged with be- ing on land occupied by Mr. James 13. West, at 11-30 p.m. on August 15th in pursuit of game.—Mr.Tomlinson, gamekeeper 'for Mr. Toft of Garston who possesses the shooting rights I said he was out on Fridsy for the purpose of netting a few rabbits for his employer. There were a few men with him and efter the nets had been set they went to Mtn the rabbits in. He (the witness) then saw two other men and afterwards heard one of his men shout.—John Reynolds, a gardener of Aston. one of the man with the previous witness, said he was outside running the rabbits up when he saw defendant and another man. Defendant said "are you on the same ground as us" and he replied "It appears so.".:One of Mr.Tomlinson's sons Came up and they went for the man. He (witness) caught the prisoner and the other man got away. Prisoner had in his cossession the nets and pegs prodaced.—Prisoner pleaded guilty and was fined 103. and 7s. 4d. costs or in de. fault 7 days.

div.head: RELEASE OF A. GLASGOW DYNAMITARD.
div.p: THE RELEASE OF A. GLASGOW DYNAMITARD.

The" Glasgow Herald " has had an interview with Devany, the convict who was released on Monday from Portland Prison. Devany arrived in Glasgow on Monday night. He is described as being about five feet six or seven inches in height,well built and healthy looking,and waeldreased in a grey frieze suit with billyeock hat. Pie was the first passenger to leave the train. No one was in waiting to meet him,for his friends,who had been expecting him earlier in the evening, had evidently given up hope of his arrival. On stepping on to the platform he looked about him in bewilderinent.ansl when asked his name he at once acknowledged thalMe was Devaire. In the course of conversation he stated that he had been away for thirteen years. " I was informed three weeks ago," he said, in answer to further ques- tions, " that I was to be liberated. I was then sent to the hospital to be fed up and that my hair might grow. (He has a short brown beard turning grey). I was taken to the railway station in a covered van. A warder accompanied me to the station and came a part of the way with me. He paid my fare, and I have £6 which I made while in prison." " You are married ?"—"Yes; and have five children." " Have you seen your wife ? ' —"No ; I would not have taken her to you place." "Are your family alive?" "I hope so,but san't tell." "You look well." was next remarked.—" Oh, yes," said Devany " Portland is not such a bad place. I did not get on well for the first three years ; but they know how to deal with you there. I was put on short allowance of food, and nearly lost my sight in consequence of the punish- ment I get. For the last ten years I have got on pretty well." " Had you abundance of food ?"—" Oh, yes, plenty of food." "Of what did it consist ?" "We had a pound of potatoes', six ounces of bread, and four ounces meat daily for dinner." "To what work were you nut ?"—" I had worked here as a quay lanourer, but I was handy with my hands, and at first I was em- ployed in the joiner's shop, and for a number of years I have been in the blacksmith's shop." " Did you know how time nagged ?"—Oh, yes, we had always two days both at Christmas, but we got no news, and knew nothing of what was passing outside." " You have not heard that Parnell is dead ?"—" No. Is he dead ? That is a pity." "You know that rit'Cann has teem released?" "Yea. We saw and recognised each other, but were never allowed to speak. The prigs' have raps and signs by which they communicate with each other, but we had no signals of that kind. I saw Daly in hospital. He had been unwell. All the prisoners have been liber- ated exeept M'Dermott. I ,ion't think he will get out for a while. I never saw Mr. Redmond or any other member of Parliament during the time I was in prison. I am very glad to be at liberty again, though Portland is not such a had rlace." At the close of the interview Devany proceeded to the Central Police Office in order to report himself, in terns of the ticket-of-leave regula- tions.

div.head: CLAIM BY A WARRINGTON DRAPER.
div.p: CLAIM BY A WARRINGTON DRAPER.
A QUESTION OF LIABILITY BETWEEN HUSBAND AND WIFE.

At Warrington County Court on Thursday, an action was brought by Mr. W. Hodgkinson of Bridge-street, to recover the sum of £3 13s. for articles of clothing sup- plied to Miss Beatrice Dutton, daughter of Wm. Dutton, licensed victualler, Bank Quay.—Defendant denied his liability as he had not authorised his wife—who ordered the goods— to pledge his credit.—Mr. Brown appeared for plaintiff and Mr. Forshaw (Messrs. Davies and For- shaw) for the defendant.—David Taylor, an assistant at Hodekineon's,proved the ordering of the goods. He was requested by the plaiatiff to go and collect the account which was now sued for from Mr. Dutton. The latter said he knew nothing about it. The daughter said her mother had bought the cloth- ing for her as a present. Miss D tton was the stepdaughter of Mrs. Dutton.—Eliztbeth Dutton stated that she was the wife of the defendant but was now living away from him. She remembered going and ordeeieg an opera cloak and bodice from Mr. Hodgkin- son's shop. Her husband ; knew she paid money out of the common purse. She gave her daughter the orders to go to Flocigkinson's. She had no separate estate whatever. She had been to Messrs. Dutton in Sankey- street and paid £l7. 6d. for a hat for her daughter. She also paid for the goods when they came in. Her husband never said anything when the opera cleak came in.— Cross-examined by Mr. Forshaw she said when the opera cleakiwas bought it was on the occasion of Miss Dutton's 21st birthday. Miss Dutton's father allowed her ss. a week.—Mr. Forshaw said that the first intimation they got of this account was five weeks ago. The defendant would swear that he never author- ised his wife to pledge his credit when he allowed her so much a week. Mrs. Dutton could not pledge her hushand'e credit unless for necessiries and were net necessaries.—William Dutton gtohoatshe was a licensed victualler carrying on business at Bank Quay, Warrington. His wife never said anything to him about ordering the articles. He never heard about it until five weeks ago when the account came from Mr. Hodgkinson. He allowed his wife £2 a week. His daughter was a barmaid with him and received 55. per week. She had to provide for her- self on that sum.—By Mr. Browne: He never remem- bered seeing the opera cloak. He never took £5O a week at the "Bowling Green" Inn. He had never seen the fur tippet. He was away in Denbigh at the time the articles were ordered by his wife, who got the money out of the drawer.—Beatrice Dutton said shs was the daughter of the defendant and Mrs. Dutton was her step-mother. On the occasion of her 21st birthday, Mrs. Dutton said that she would make her a present instead of her going zo a party. She went with her to Hodekiuson's and was measured for an opera cloak and bodice. Mrs. Dutton ordered the cloak and bodice to be put down to her account. Her father did not know anything about it. She was allowed 51. a week which she had been receiving for about 12 months. She bought her own clothes out of £1 a month.—Cross-examined by Mr. Browne : She supposed her father was going to pay ter the party. When her step-mother was at horne she was allowed all the threepenny bits and would probably pay for the articles out of that. She did not expect her father was going to pay as he said he would not pay for anything after she was 21. She wore the cloak at the Coneerva- tive hall. Her father did not go with her to the second Conservative ball. He saw her going. Her father made objection to the tippet but not the hat. Her mother paid for a pair of boots from Mr. Roberts' shop, Bridge- street. She also Paid for a jacket witness was wearing, from Lord's in Bridge-street and which cost £1 153. Od. It was bought twelve months ago last Christmas. Mrs. Dutton ordered everything fer the ball.—His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff. He said this was one of the cases in which it was not very easy to arrive at the true facts of the case as there was not a very pleasant feeling between husband and wife.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held on Wednesday morning at the Union Workhouse. Mr. G. Pilling presided, and there were also present,Dr. Patterson, Messrs. W. Houghton, T. Halton, J. Billinge. A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, J. Ball, John Dignum, W. Hickman, John Houghton, T. B. Mal- kin, G Thompson, J. W. Knowles, Clarke' J. C. Sutton (clerk). S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (Work- house Master), and A. Wright (superintendent of Pad- gate Schools.)
POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS.

The CLERK said that, at the request of the Warrington Postmaster, be had snit him a list of the names of the overse-rs of the poor and the assistant overseers of all the townships in the union to facilitate the delivery of letters only officially addressed. The Postmaster had acknowledged the receipt of the list.

div.head: VACCINATION RITUIIN9.
div.p: VACCINATION RITUIIN9.
The CLERK produced the returns of the vaccination officers far the period Ist July to 31st December, 1895. He had sent copies of the returns to the Local Govern- ment Board, as requir.A.
THE ESTIMATES.

The CLERK laid before the Board the estimate of con- tributions by the parishes that would be required for the half year, ending Lady Day, 1897. but he said that, as usual, the estimate would rem sin in abeyance for the further consideration of the Board, when they would be in possession of the supplemental lists. Further, he was not in receipt of the country rate, and that e could Rot include it in his report. Me would lay the estimate before the Bo ,rd at the next meeting.

div.head: THIC AGRICULTURAL RATING ACT
div.p: THIC AGRICULTURAL RATING ACT

_ The CLERK said he had riv.-el voluminous orders and forms of financial and ctAtistieti statements re- quired to he made under the A!!rinnlturAl R tteg Act. In answer to Mr. Billinge, Mr. Sutton said th, new rating system would come intr fore,. in M.irch next year. His estimate was hssed on the pr,sent rate ible value, as if the Act had not been passed.

TEE EXTENSION OF THE BOROUGH. The CLERK said things were further complicated by the extension of the Union following on the extension of the borough. The Order came into operation on the Ist November. Their accounts all closed for the half-year at Michaelmas. so that there would be one month be- twoen the clorinr, of their accounts and the time for taking over the portions of the Runcorn Union which came into the borcmgh. With a view to understanding what procedure was proposed under the Agricultural Ra.tine Act and in regard to those 'portions of the Run- cern Union transferred to Warrineton, he had seen Mr. Ashton.the clerk to the Runcorn Union, and after con- siderahlm conversation they decided to ask their respec- tive Hoards to authoripe them to act for them and inntually adjust the matters that require.! adjustment. The Bard authorised Mr. Sutton to act for them a• mentioned.

OLD AGE PENSIONS. The CLERK stated that he had received a letter from the Sleaford Union asking the Board to support a reso- lution urging upon the Government the necessity of pro- viding old age pensions from the Imperial Xxchequer, so that deserving poor may be raised above the position of common paupers. The Clerk added that this was a sensible resolution enough, but he thought it was one of those matters that could be best dealt with in general conference. .

CATION OF PAUPERS. At a meeting of the Rouse Committee, Mr. Moorson reported having inspected the Workhouse. The COM- mittee, after consideration of a circular letter from the Local Government Board upon the subject of the classi- fication of indoor paupers, whilst favourable to the pur- pose of that letter, were of opinion that any material departure from existing arrangements would be best deferred until after the erection of the intended new in- firmary, when facilities for improved classification will arise. The committee, after considering the officers' diet table and having compared it with the allowances to officers at other workhouses, recommended certain changes set forth on a list. Mr. A. .J. JOLLEY moved the adoption of the minntes, and remarked that they could do little in the way of further claeeifying the paupers in view of the fact that the premises next year would be very much upset with the new buildings, so the committee thought the matter had better stand over. The question of the officers' dietary was a very important one. It had been con- sidered three times by the committee,so that there could be no suggestion that they were endeavouring to rush the matter throegh. They feund that the officers at the workhouse all round were less liberally treated than in any other union they had been Ds communication with. They therefore thought it desirable to revise the table. There was a difference between the dietary at the work- house and the schools, but they proposed te make it more uniform.—Mr. Knowles : Which got the best ? Mr. A. J.Jolley said there were slight differences at both places.—Mr. John Houghtor asked how the dietary compared with Birkenhead.—Mr. A. J. Jolley : Oh it is not nearly an good.—Mr. Hickman seconded the motion for the adoption of the minutes, and it was passed.

A DEARTH OE NURSES. div.head: DEATH FRO3I DOG BITES. -- A GIRL'S DESPERATE STRUGGLE WITH A ST. BERNARD.
div.p: THE DEATH FRO3I DOG BITES. -- A GIRL'S DESPERATE STRUGGLE WITH A ST. BERNARD.

Mr. Tihhits, deputy coroner for West Cheshire. held an inquest on Tuesday afternoon at the Abbotsford Hotel, Seaeombe, on the body of Christopher Ellswolth, 49 years of are, a bookkeeper, who resided at 21, Rud- grave Square, Egrrmont, and whose death resulted from severe injuries caused by his St. Bernard dog worrying him.--Amelia J. Ellsworth, daughter of the deceased, stated that on Bank Holiday her father went into the back yard to see his dog. a St. Bernard. She went with him, as eh? was the only one who could manage the animal, and she took a whip with her. The dog got hold of her father's leg and pulled him to the ground, keeping him there for a few minutes. She tried to beat the deg off with the whip, hut was unable to do so effectually. She got kim off three times, and ence got her hand in its mouth and tried to break its jaw, but could not suceeed. She got her father into the house, but the dog had still hold of his leg. She gave the dog a knock en the head and tried to crush it between the doer. They had had the dog since it was about two months old. It was all right at times, but was inclined te be savage; its mother was a savage animal. Wit- ness's sister fetched Dr. Crook, and a nurse was aka in attendance on her father, who was removed on Thurs- day last to the Seacombe Cottage Hospital. Her father did nothing to the dog to cause it to turn upon him. Be had been to the lairages that day and had some blood upon his boot, and she thought the dog must have smelt this when it attacked him.—Replying to the jury, the witness said that the dog, which was a year and ten months old, had only been nut two or three times. The first time it was out it knocked a child down. It wae not kept fastened un in the yard.--Sarah Collins,matron of the Seacombe Cot4-age Hospital, stated that Mr. Ells- worth was admi ted to the institution on the 13th in- stant suffering from wounds and dog bites on the left Bodied on the Monday from exhaustion, conse- quent upon persistent sickness and the dog bites. He suffered terrible agony—The jury returned a verdict that death was due to the effects of the dog bites.
