Early on NlQnday morning a serious subsidence oc- curred just outside the town of Northwich, a portion of the Warrington main road being eng,ulphed.A hole thirty feet in diameter and at least sixty feet deep was formed, and for some time vehicular traffic was impeded. The lower part of the cavity quickly filled with water, and cracks for some distance gave evidenee that a further and greater sinkage is probable.

div.head: NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

Oa Sunday afternoon as Mr. &etas, of Bedford, was riding home on his bicycle from Ampthill, he saw a tramp get up from the side of the road and come to- wards him. Thinking the man was going to beg cep- pore or tobacco,Mr. Nuns slowed up,and put his hand his pocket for a penny. Instead of waiting for the cop- per,the tramp struck him a violent blow on the jaw, knocking him senseless off his machine. Mr. Binns was found later on in an unconscious condition,and was con- veyed to his home. A tramp was subsequently ar- rested by Constable Javeas and brought before the magistrate on Monday charged with the assault. Super- intendent Quenly said other charges of a similar nature would probably be preferred against the man, who was remanded.

The Press Association states that further diplomatic correspondence relating to the outrages in Armenia will be issued sbortly,from which it will nndeubtedly appear that they originated at Yildiz Kiosk, and were approved by the Sultan, in order to check the apparently rapid development of the Young Turkish or Reform party,not from any dread of a serious attempt by the Armenians to revolt. The latter were massacred as a warning to the former of what they might expect if they continued their revolutionary propaganda. The despatches will show that it has new been ascertained that not less than 100,000 Armenians—men, women, and children—have been massacred.

The potent " penny in the slat" seems most potent in connection with gas meters. Fifty thousand slot meters and 37,400 cooking stoves issued therewith have been fixed during the last four years by /he South Metro- politan Gas Company, which illuminatss only about a sixth of London. One result is that small dealers in wood, coal, and lamp oil complain that their trade is be- ing ruined; while the chimney sweepers have gone so far as to send a deputation with a protest to the com- pany. When one puts his penny in the meter he gets 27 feet of gas— a rate of 3s. id. per 1,000 The average annual consumption through each slot meter is 12,000 feet where only light is wanted, but 19,000 feet where cooking is also on the programme. Of course the com- pany has had to exercise ingenuity against the demand for free gas. French pennies were their first trouble. Now the slot meter rejects them. A penny fastened to a string and drawn out when the gas was no longer wanted has been met by an arrangement which cute the string. The soapy penny. sticking in the machinery and keeping the gas "on " has also been rendered use- less ; so that now the company's only anxiety is to be paid before customers remove.

After having amassed a colossal fertune by the sale of champagne, M. Auban Moet says the " felegraph's " Paris correspondent, has shown himself to be one of the most generous of philanthropists. During his lifetime he gave anonymously, as has since been ascertained, £16,000 to a provincial hospital which he built. lie has now in his last will and testament instructed his widow to hand over £25,000 to the same institution, thus bringing the donation up to 1,000,01101. To the Charitable Association of Epernay the testator leaves £4,000, and on the occasion of his funeral, which took place on Monday 10,000 f is to be distributed among the poor of the same town. The famous champagne manufacturer has asked to be buried simply, without towers or wreaths.

With reference to the career of M. Thome, formerly a stonemason and later a millionair., who died a few days ago in Paris, the "Deily News" correspondent says : "M. Thorne was born in Provence, and came to Paris to look for work over fifty years ago, when Baron FlaossmAnn was the new-made Prefect of the Seine. He fell in with Thome, and, seeing him full of ideas, en- couraged him. This led to Thorne's giving him advice about the capacities of Chaillot, the Trocadero, and the Marbcsuf district for enlarging Paris. He then drew up a plan, which Haussmann adopted, for opening up these districts with main and secondar3 streets. Thorne at once speculated on money lent in return for information he was able to give to great financiers. He bought acres on acres of waste ground, and slum habitations without end, and became the greatest holder of ground for build- ing sites in what Is now the most fashienable west-end part of the capital. One of his daughters married M. Chins, the great Grasse distiller of scents from flowers. She had a dowry proportionate to her father's wealth. Her daughter in turn married in 1894 President Caruot's son Ernest. Thorne's two sons are, in point of wealth and position, magnates. The personality of the former mason is valued at over £2,000,000. Thome and his wife never aspired to be genteel,' much less aristocra- tic. They lived in handsome style, entertained hospit- ably, and kept open house for relatives and old friends who had or had not risen in the wend. Though Thome did so well under the Empire, he was a Republican, but of a moderate type. To the end he looked the stone- mason, and in the country he always were a blouse on week days."

American wonders never cease. A pair of 4. well- known citizens "of Sin Francisco, prominent athletes, NI hose stamina is vouched for by several physicians,and whose social standing is testified to by several persons of importance,are about to attempt to cross the American continent crawling on their hands and knees. They will grasp handblocks and wear pneumatic pads on their !mom while their heels will be suspended from their belts:by a sort of harness,and their eyes covered by gog- gles. Their feat is the principal subject of illustration and comment in the latest issue of the New York Sun- day " World." This is going back to the ape with a vengeance.

It is a remarkable and somewhat disconcerting fact that the death-rate from cancer has increased and ir increasing. On this subject Mr. W. Roger Williams, of the Middlesex Hospital, has some timely remarks in the "Medical Chronicle," although they are, as he states, to a large extent a repetition of views that he has on pre- vious occasions laid before his professional colleagues. In 1840 cancer was held responsible for the deaths of 177 per million living, and in 1894 of 713 per million living. "Thus the proportionate cancer morality is ROW more than four times greater than it was half a century ago, and in this respect it stands absolutely alone. Moreover the same tendency is observable in all civilised lands, so that, unless checked, cancer may be expected to become one of the Commonest diseases of modern communities." Mr. Williams lays much stress upon the influence of food. " Probably no single factor," he says, " is more 'potent in determining the outbreak of cancer in the predisposed than high feeding. There can be no doubt that the greed for food manifested by modern communi- ties is altogether out of proportion to their present re- quirements. Many indications point to the gluttonous consumption of meat, which is such a characteristic feature of the age' as likely to be especially harmful in this respect." And in this connection he points out that our countrymen are the worst sinners since the con- sumption of flesh meat in England is more than double the present average for the rest of Europe.

A spacial meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council was held on Wednesday at the Union Work- house, there being present Messrs. J. Ball (presiding), .1. W. Knowles. T. Halton, J. Houghton, G. Thompson. J. Dignum, S. Sutton (clerk), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector). The CLERK said he had received a letter from Mr. Forster, clerk to the Penketh Parish Council, to say that the action of the Parish Council in regard to the water supply had been approved without dissent at a rate- payers' meeting. He (the clerk) was instructed by the Streets Committee to see the Town Clerk and ask for the work to be proceeded with at once. MI now wanted a resolution passed confirming what had been done.— Mr. Dignutn moved that the arrangement with the Cor- poration be approved.—Mr. Halton seconded and the motion was passed.—This concluded the business.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC.

During the week ended August 14./93 vessels, with an aggregate net registered tonnage of 44,413 tons, entered and cleared from the port of Manchester, as compared with 146 vessels of 43,724 net registered tons in die pre- ceding week. Of these, 43 vessels of 22,600 tons entered from or cleared for foreign ports, and 152 vessels of 21,813 tons arrived or sailed coastwise. The principal feature in the week's traffic was the activity in th 3 Bal- tic trade. Amongst the more important arrivals were steamers and one sailing ship with timber from the Bal- tic and North America, eight vessels from the north of France with flints, a steamer from Bonieaux and Nantes with large consignments of copper, wine, fruit, and pre- serves ; general cargoes from Rouen, Treport, Boulogne, Ghent, Antwerp, Rotterdam, and Copenhagen, and wheat from the Dardanelles. Steamers cleared outwards for Brazil, Alexandria, St. Petersburg, Christiania, Copenhagen, Hamburg, Rotterdam, Antwerp, Treport, Rouen, Paris, and Bordeaux, and sailing vessels for Helsingborg, Gibraltar, Halifax, N.S., and West Bay. The Dublin steamer on Friday disembarked 150 cattle. 65 sheep, and five horses, and a large consignment of Canadian sheep and cattle is due in a day or two.

div.head: AUSTRALIAN CRICKETERS AT
div.p: THE AUSTRALIAN CRICKETERS AT
HOME AND ABROAD.

"The ninth Australian team is a standing witness to the democratic tendencies of colonial life," writes Mr. Fred McKenzie, in the August Number of the" Windsor Magazine." "Our southern dominions know nothing of the sharp division between 'gentlemen 'and 'players' that time-honoured custom has sanctioned in England. In Australia cricket is a hobby, not a business, and all the great players have their occupations apart from the game. Except once a year when colony is pitted against colony to obtain the supremacy of the continent, and on special occasions like the visit of an English team, matches only take place on Saturday afternoons, from half-past two till six, when there is a general half-holi- day. The professional cricketer is practically unknown and though a few men are given eenetant employment. on the principal fields, they take no part in centests or any note, merely, fagging 'for the players. Everyone who can do good work is welcome on equal terms with the others, altogether apart from his social position. Thus in the team now visiting us the members are drawn from very varied callings. Several are civil ser- vants, and three are. barristers and solicitors. Banking has its representative in Trumble and bricklaying in Jones the Demon Clement Hill is preparing to be at engineer, Iredale is a surveyor, Graham's fancy lightly turns to dentistry, and Darling is at the head of a sports , depot. This will be my last visit to England, and I hope to make it a good one,' George Giffen declared to his friends before leaving Adelaide, and he is going the right way to keep his intention. No antipodean cricke- ter has greater fame in England than the Australian Grace'; but to see George Giffen at his best one has be witness his performances at the Adelaide Oval or in Sydney with the theremometer re- gistering 1.06 degrees in the shade. The Eeglish climate does not suit him, and our treacherous winds and moist air are more than he can stand with comfort. The change from the heat of an .Australian March to the bleakness of an English April put hirn out of condition immediately on his arrival here. No man can do his best when his head is splitting and his eyes are burning with an influenza cold, and that has been Giffen's state during at least part of the last three months. It may be said that most ot the Australians, with the exceptio; of one or two like Johns, find our climate trying. The heat they do not mind, though they would prefer the dry scorching atmosphere of the south to our muggy June temperature; but the sudden variations from heat to cold and the constant rains are not altogether to their taste." " The selection of the Australian team was a task compared to which the choice of a ministry is a trifle. Every colony is firmly convinced that it has enough good men to fill at least half the places in the team, and this:: nothing but the jealousy of the other colonies could pre- vent this honour being given to it. The duty of selec- tion lies finally in the hands of the Australasian Coutici!, a body of twelve members drawn in equal parts from each of the three principal crieketing colonies, New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia. The Council leaves the work in the hands of a committee, composed this year of Messrs. G. Giffen, W. Bruce and T. Garret,. When the names picked by this committee were mule known early last February a cry of disappointment went up from all over Australia. Eack colony asserted that rank injustice had been done to it, and some critics went so far as to say that even it the team won every match in England still they would be a bad choice, be- cause those left out could have done much better. No one could understand the omission of the tames ot Clement Hill, Turner the Terror, and. A. E. Trott, whose record against Stoddart's party secured him such haw, It will be remembered that Turner was kept out of the great Avglo-Australian inatcli as Melbourne last year, aud after all was over Stocidart went up to him and solemnly thanked him for havins: contributed to the English success—by his absenes I Many appeals wee made to the Australasian Council to overrule its Cott, mittee, but the Council (wisely, its it has since proved), remained firm except on two points, C,iernent added to the team as a fourtesnth member at the moment, and Harry, the famous fast Itiowler, iisd• make way for another, J. J. Kelly, greatly to his wrate and disappointment."

THE ELECTION OF A DISTRICT COUNCILLOR.

Contrary to general expectation, the vacant seat on the District Council, caused by the death of Mr. James Smith, has been filled without a contest. The closing day for nomination was Tuesday, and the only name submitted as a candidate was that of Dr. J. N. Patterson, who represents the ward on the Board of Guardians. The Doctor has therefore been declared elected. Four nomination papers were anded in in his favour, the proposers in each case being the Rev. E. W. W. Kaye, Mr. J. W. Thorp, Mr. E. Bunting and Mr. W. Mills.

The usual weekly session of the Hope of Earles- town Lo Ige was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street,on Monday evening. Bro. W. Wilson, C.T., presided over a good attendance of members, and about 20 visitors from the Ashton Excelsior and Ebenezer Lodges received a hearty welcome. One candidate was proposed for membership. Final arrangements for the District Lodge Session to be held in Earlestown on Saturday next were re- ported upon. Business over,the visitors were called upon,when earnest and encouraging addresses were given by Bro. James Woods,of Earlestown,and Bros. J. Bowler and Hughes of Ashton. Songs, readings, &c., were given by Bros. Speakman, Jenkins, Jack- son, Hughes, and others. Hearty thanks were ac- corded the visitors to which Bro. Woods responded, and a very encouraging session was closed in the usual way. TFIE INDUSTRIAL CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. The 143rd quarterly meeting of the members of this society was held in the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening. Mr. D. Forester presided, and there was a good attendance. The report and balance sheet were submitted, and congratulations were offered upon a satisfactory increase in trade and a successful quarter. The cash receipts amounted to £4,192 123. 914., being an increase on last quarter of £l3l is. 91, and compared with the corresponding p.riod last year (12 weeks) shows an increase of £534 93. 211. The net profits available for dividend on purchases are £623 18 6i1., which it was proposed to distribute as follows :—To pay a dividend of 2s. 91. in the £ to members, which would require £565 103. 91.; and Is. 41. in the ..E to non-members, requiring Bs., leaving a balance of ..E35 to carry to the dividend reserve fund, and £22 19s. 914. to the contingent fund. During the quarter 25 new members have been admitted, and four struck off, leasing 970 on the hooks, 642 of whom 'sad brought in checks. The report and balance sheet were adopted. It was decided to leave the question of secretaries' remuneration in the hands of the committee, with an understanding that they had not to exceed the expenditure in the department for the previous quarter. Messrs. W. Clars and T. Holliday were re-appointed on the Committee of Management, and Mr. J. Gooding was /e-appointed auditor. It was decided to subscribe the usual sum to the Technical Instruction Class?.a.

div.head: IitEWTON CHORAL AND ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY. –
div.p: IitEWTON CHORAL AND ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY. -
ANNUAL MmETING.

The annual general meeting of the members of the above society was held in St. Peter's schoolroom on Monday evening. Dr. J. W. Watkins presided and there was a fair attendance, amongst whom were noticed Messrs. R. Barlow, J. Singleton, J. Owen, Mrs. Clare, Royse, Miss Pardey, and Miss Watkins. The Chairman after expressine regret at the absence of the president. said he bad very few words to say, far the business of the meeting he thought might be en- trusted largely to their active and energetic secretary, Mr. Glover. At all events he could congratulate them upon having arrived at the end of their first year, and achieved perhaps a greater measure of success than they ventured to anticipate a year ago. They had bad two Concerts, and he thoueht he might say unhesitatingly that musically they were both a success, moutarily they were not. Perhaps after tneir experience of last year they might gain some wisdom and have the concert at a better time than when they were compelled to have it last spring. They had spoken of their lose but they also deplored the lose of one of the warmest-hearted friends ; one who before the societyl was established took great interest in its being brought about and bet for his long and serious illness, which ended in his lamented death, he (the speaker) was certain would have proved one of the firmest,largest and warmest supporters of the society. He moved the following resolution :--ee The Newton-le-Willaws Choral and Orchestral Seeley hereby record their sense of the great loss they have sustained by the death of Mr. James Smith, of Brookside, and also tender their deepest syme. pathy with Meseemith and family in their bereavement." Mrs. Clara Royse seconded and it was carried. Mr. James Glover, secretary, presented the statement of accounts which showed the total receipts from all sources amounted to £37 2s. id, and the expenditure £36 171. 81., leaving a balance of 4s. 51 in hand. The loss in the second concert held in April was £5 3s. 9d. So far as the musical part of the session was concerned it was distinctly a success al- though they suffered in several ways Ihreugh circum- stances over which they had no control. They had reason to complain of the attendance of the members. It was not quite so good as it might be. During the first part of the session,out of 60 members threequartere of the number were present,and during the second part about two-thirds. He thought they might improve on that next time. Mr. R. Berton moved the adoption of the balance sheet, Mr. Owen seconded, and the motion was carried enanirnously. On the motien of Mr. J. Singleton and seconded by r. W. Turner, the Hon. T. W. Legh,M.P., was elected preeirieut of the society. Dr. Watkins was unanimously re-appointed vice-pre- sident on the motion of Mr. Glover, and seconded by Mrs. Royce. The retiring committee, Mrs. E. T. Beene, , Mrs. Reyse,Miss Wekins, and Pileeere. Feirelough, lein.on, and Singletno were re-appointed en bloc, and the e name of Mr. Hindley Smith was afterwards added. Captain Rey was re-appointed treasurer on the ' motion of Mr. Barton, and Mr. James Glover was re- ' eleeted hon. secretary. Miss Watkins was appointed Librarian. The Secretary intimated that the cemrnittee had arranged to hold the weekly rehearsals on Monday evenings instead of Thurs- day and it was intended to start on September 21st. A vote of thanks was heartily accorded the Chairman. who in ackoowledging the compliment promised them that in a musical sense they would work with a will and work in unison, hoping out of the unison to produce harmony in the society.

A SEQUEL TO THE COIL STRIKE.-MONEY LENT OR MONEY EARNED? -

Before his HO-1-1-our Judge Wynne Ffoulkes at the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, Mr. James Grace, of Messrs. Grace and Co.. claimed from Themes Bradshaw, a former employe of the firm, £8 35., which he said he had lent defendant when hard up in the coal strike.—Mr.lirowne repre- sented defendant.—Mr.Grace said that in the spring ot 1893 his works were stopped and not wanting to lose altogether the defendant,plaintiff lent him 30s. every week to keep him going. Altogether he had lent £l5 15s. Defendant pertormed several small jobs for him in that time but was paid for them and those payments left a balance on the whole sum lent of .£8 35., the amount claimed. Re refrained from pressing for the debts as defendant had other accounts to pay. Defendant left the town and was away 24 years. When he returned plaintiff deter- mined to get his money and brought this action.— Defendant denied that he was paid separately for the jobs done. He receiving 30s. a week as stated. —John Bradshaw, son of defendant, said he never heard of his father borrowing money from Mr. Grace. Witness worked for Mr. Grace but received nothing, as plaintiff paid his father.—Mr. Browne said that was his case.—His Honour said whatever money was advanced to defendant was advanced to him for odd jobs done about the place. He would therefore give judgment for the defendant.

Robert Garnett and Sons, Warrington, travelled to Blackpool on Saturday, a goodly number of the workmen's wives and sweet- hearts accompanying the party. The weather was everything that could be desired, and the utmost advantage was taken of the favourable circum- stances to visit the various places of amusement. After tea, which was provided at the Central Tem- perance Hotel, Mr. Nicholson, as chairman of the gathering, in a few well chosen words proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the firm. He spoke of his long connection with it, and the esteem in which Messrs. Garnett and Sons were held by their work- men. Other speakers followed in support, and the motion was carried with acclamation. Mr. R. E. Garnett, in thanking them, said it gave him great pleasure to be present. He felt that they were in a very great measure indebted to their workmen for the prosperity which had all along attended their efforts. He hoped that the good feeling which existed between the firm and their employ& would continue. Ile spoke of the position they, as a firm, held in the cabinet trade of the country, and said he hoped that next year they would have more work- men in their employ to accompany them on the occasion of their annual outing. (Applause.) The party returned home in detachments, owing to the crowded state of the railway arrangements. Messrs. Garnett and Sons defrayed the travelling expenses of the employee. div.head: FOR SPOILED CAKES.
div.p: FOR SPOILED CAKES.

Before his Honour Judge Pfoulkes at the War- rington County Court on Thursday, James Eddie, confectioner,Winwick-road,Warrington, sued James Hunt, the well-known jumper, and who formerly kept the " Shalinon and Chesapeake' for 30s. for damages for trespass.-11r. Browne for the plaintiff, explained that his client rented a bakehouse from the defendant, off Winwick-road, and on the Wed- nesday before Walking Day he owed 25.6 i. for rent. He went for his dinner soon after 12 o'clock leaving some Sultana and Madeira cakes baking. At 12 30 his son returned and found the bakehouse door with a padlock on. He told his father and the latter asked Mr. Hunt how it was and defendant said he should keep him out until he paid the rent. Plaintiff's son threatened to break in, and defendant then threatened that if he did he would summon him for damage. Mr. Eddie went and borrowed the amount, 2s. 6d., and paid the rent, and then entered the bakehouse. He found the wtole of the cakes burnt and un- saleable. He further discovered that some Bath buns were also spoiled. Plaintiff's two sons had missed their connection through being locked out and 15s. worth of confectionery which was already baked was also spoiled. Witnesses proved this state- ment, and the defence was practically an admission of the whole matter except that defendant thought he had a perfect right to lock the door.—His Honour gave verdict for 30s. the amount claimed by plain- tiff.

Frank Taylor,a labourer,23 years of age,was executed at Birmingham on TueAday for the murder of a little girl named Mary I.4.±wis. He made no confession, but wrotea letter to his mother bidding her farewell. There was no doubt of his guiltsor that he was a criminal of a peculiarly atrocious type.

The Lymm Volunteers assembled at headquarters on Saturday, and headed by the band, under Sergeant Neigle, marched to Cuerden Hall, Thelwall, the resid- ence of Mr. H. A. Naylor, who had invited the company to spend the day there as his guests. Captain J. E. G. groves, who was in command, marched the company to the front of the hall, where they were kindly received by Mr. and Miss Naylor, and made heartily welcome. Among the invited guests of Mr. Naylor were the Mayor of Warrington, Dr. Sherratt, Mr. and Miss Dale (of Lon- don), &c. Immediately after the arrival the men were supplied with refreshments, and soon all were busy playing games, such as tennis, bowls, &c., and before long a goodly list of entries for the sports was secured. The sports included 220yds., and 440yds., and three- legged races, and tugs of war. In the latter the single men teams were pulled over the mark in grand style, and the final between the two married teams was an equally exciting event. Tea was served in the Temperance Hall. Tea over Miss Naylor presented the prizes to the successful competitors, who were heartily cheered. An entertainment followed, which included songs by Mr. Dale, Miss Kirkpatrick, Mr. Naylor, Private Smith and Sergeant J. Hatton, mandoline and autoharp duets by Bandsmen Allgayer (father and son), piano solos by Miss Dale, and a vocal duet by Mr. and Miss Naylor. After the concert, Cap- tain Groves proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. and Miss Naylor. This was seconded by the Mayor of War- rington in a few appropriate words, and enthusiastically carried. Mr. Naylor, in response, said he was always glad to see the volunteers at his house and :hoped that they would be able to come again next year. (Apnlause.) Before leaving the men were provided with tea and coffee, and as the home journey was commenced the band struck up" Auld Lang Syne " and hearty cfri were given for Mr. and Miss Naylor.

t.Z PADGATE. 1-`1,.. 2. - ,41'21•A,341:',Ee2 DEATH AND I' jIN,FRAL OF MRS: JOSEPH HOUGHTON:— The remains of the la.tri Mrs.-Elfitbgth'lloughtoe, relict of the late Mr. Joseph Houghton, of the Wilgreaves, Woolston, were interred in the Warrington Cemetery on Monday. The deceased lady, who was the mother of Mr. William Houghton J.P., chairman of the Warrington District Council,was widely known and highly respected amongst a large circle of friends. She had been attended in her illness by Dr. White, of Warrington, but the cause of death was natural decay. The body was taken at noon on Monday to Christ Church, Padgate, where a short service was conducted by the Rev. J. J. Langbarn, at which a number of friends, apart from the mourners, were present. After the service tha funeral procession proceeded to the cemetery, where the body was interred and the service concluded by the Rev. J. J. Langharn. The chief mourners were—Messrs. Joseph Houghton, Isaac Houghton, John Houghton, Thomas Houghton, James Houghton and William Houghton, J.P., (sons) ; Thomas Bennett and I. Swinton (sons-in-law) ; and a number ef other relatives. Amongst a large number of others present at the church and in the cemetery were Dr. White, Mr. William Bennett (Lyndhurst), Mr. Wil- liam Royston, Mr. H. Hoult,Mr. H. Taylor (representing Mr. Frederick Taylor), and Mr. P. Wright. The wreaths numbered 27, and included several beautiful floral tributes, the chief one being a large and magnificent cross of flowers, measuring several feet in length, from deceased's sans and daughters, which bore the tollowing inscription :—" The united tribute of love and affection of her family to a loving, affectionate, and exemplary mother. _ _
Leave we now our mother, sleeping." Father in Thy gracious keeping. The funeral arrangements were in the hands of Messrs. J.and W. Dutton, of Sankey-itreet.

div.head: IHE CHIEF JUSTICE IN AMERICA.'
div.p: IHE CHIEF JUSTICE IN AMERICA.'

Tlae Lord Chief Justice of England attended on Thurs- day the Law Congress at Saratoga Springs, New York, and delivered an interesting address on international law. Having spoken of the many things which English- men and Americans had in common and the "crimson thread" of kinship between them, his Lordship dealt seriatim with the questions of what international law is, its sources, the ethical standard to which it ought to conform, and the characteristics of its modern developments. With regard to codification, he said it would have a tendency to arrest progress, and he did not at present advocate it. The tendency in modern international law was to mitigate the horrors of war, to humanise or to make less inhuman its methods, and to narrow the area of its consequential evils. This, he considered, was largely due to the policy of American statesmen and the moral influence of American jurists. In spite of all,however,there was war in the air. Nations armed to the teeth prated of peace, but there was no sense of peace. If there was no war, there was at best but an armed peace. The cost of normal armaments had of late years enormously increased, and, he asked, when would Gpvernments learn the lesson that wisdom and justice in policy were a stronger security than weight of armament? He recognised the difficulties of the Question, hut it was hardly too much to say that arbitration might be fitly applied in the case of by far the largest number of questions which led to inter- national differences. He admitted, however, that at this stage the question of the constitution of a perma- nent tribunal was not ripe for practical discussion, nor would it be until the majority ef the Great Powers had given in their adhesion to the principle.

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
VIADUCT INSTITUTE CLUB.

The members ofthis dull played their annual handi- cap for Mr.J. W. Thorp's prize on Saturday, under favourable conditions. The entrants numbered 38, which is the largest number this season. The green was again in excellent condition, with the result that soma exceedingly good bowling was witnessed, and the efforts of the players evoked much applause from the specta- tors. The following were the prize winners :—P. Tal- bot (Mr. Thorp's prize) ; J. Green. 2 ; and J. Mitchell, 3. The prizes were presented to the successful players at the close, and a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Thorp for providing such an afternoon's sport,was accorded.

LOCAL WEDDINGS.
WEDDING AT ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH.

The marriage of Mr. John Leigh (second son of the late Mr. Peter Leigh, grocer, &c., llorsemarket-st.), to Miss Mary (Polly) Sudlow, youngest daughter of Mr. Charles Sudlow, Winwick-st., was quietly solemnized in St. John's Presbyterian Church on Tuesday morning. The bride was given away by her father, the bridesmaid being her sister, Miss Maggie Sudlow ; Mr. W. Litton acting as best man. The Rev. James Warnock, MA., 8.D., officiated. Mr. and Mrs. Leigh afterwards pro- ceeded to Grange-on-Sands, where part of the honey- moon will be spent. A large number of presents were received by the happy pair. The guests were enter- tained to breakfast and supper at the house of the bride's father.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

When the SAton team visits Warrington the match is always looked upon as a good one and spectators a2e not slow in taking their plaees round the Arpley en- closure. Saturday saw another of these annual visits and the attendance on the field was encouraging. The first match this season between the clubs took place at Sefton and resulted in an easy victory for Warrington, who were best represented by Bibby and Hampson. Both of these batsmen played on Saturday and there was some speculation as to whether they would again as- tonish the Seftonians. However, the easy win which Warrington pulled off precluded this possibility as the innings was closed at 154 for seven wickets.

The visitors went in first and the bowling was taken up by the two professionals. Connor was absent owing to illness. C. L. Jones and r. W. Stubbs were the first partners, but six runs only were on the board when Scrimshaw took Jones' leg stump. Armstrong joined Stubbs but again no stand could be made, Scrimshaw holding a return from the latter. No more runs had been chronicled when Thewlis with one of his straight mediums bowled Armstrong. With this bad opening it loaked as if the visitors were going to be dismissed early, but Storer and H. Ratcliffe brightened things up a bit. The latter however lifted Thewlis too much and was caught by Bibby. H. Tongue and A. H.Boswell both failed to keep out Scrimshaw and retired with only 40. runs up. Storer was next joined by Edwards and both began to play the bowling with conicionce. At half-3-century Crosfield relieved Thewlis and Edwards was forced to concede a catch to Bibby. He had added 22. H. Gros- venor was the next batsman but he was beaten by Serimshaw for 8. Storer still continued to hit har,i, but Thewlis resuming, he skied the ball to long field where Callon after being muck bothered by the wini man- aged to held it. Thirty-six was the total of the retiring batsman and his was the best innings of the team. Bis- hop put on 13 but his last partner, A. W. Brock could do nothing with Scrimshaw and rnade a "duck." This brought the visitors' innings to a close for 108.

Warrington opened :with S. M. Crosfield and A. C. Nelson. A good partnership was expected as the latter had recently performed well for the Colts of the county but he was beaten by Armstrong after scoring one run. J. Callon came on and with his captain began to raise the score rapidly. Both hit out well, Crosfield showing characteristic skill. Bowling changes were tried but all manner of hits care from the bats of the two players. When 69 had been reached, Callon in snatching a short run failed to reach his crease and had to retire after contributing 29 in very good style. Thewlis came in next and the bowling was changed with his appearance. Six runs had been put on when Crosfield was smartly snapped at the wicket by Brock. His 40 was compiled from unblemished cricket. Tnewlis had only reached 9 when a" yorker " from Armstrong took off the bails. W. Nelson after a stroke or two dropped the ball into Crrosvenor's hands, and the match bean almost to look douistful, especially as Podmore was caught by. the same man. G. Clarke and J. Bibby began cautiously, and after passing the hundred the left hander drove Armstrong twice for four. The game won, Clarke and he hit out finely and Bibby made 20 before being caught. G. Hampson stayed in until Clarke had reached 34, when the innings was closed for 154 runs at the expense of 7 wickets.

--- The bowling on the Warrington side was very good, both professionals shining conspicuously. Scrimshaw, especially, was very successful, and had at the close the good average of 6 Wickets for 53 runs. Thewlis took throe for 37 runs.

The Sefton cricketers wore indeed hardly used on Saturday for at home and away their first and second teams were badly beaten by the Warrington elevens. At Sefton the two second teams were playing, and the homesters had the advantage of being the first to make use of a good wicket. They were :however un- able to do much apinst the bowling of Silcock, Reddy, and Unsworth, who dismissed the team for 102. J. Morrow, who made 29, was the only batsman who could score steadily,and his innings was terminated by a catch in Duckworth's hands. The bowling came out as fol- lows: Silcock, 4 wickets for 40 runs, Roddy, 2 for 32, and Unsworth, 3 for 14. Fielding and wicket keeping was also of a creditable nature.

Warrington opened the inninas with C. R. Adamson and W. M. Silcock. The fomer was bowled for 11, but his partner drove the leather in fine style and contributed 42 runs, the highest score of the match, before being caught by J. H. Rodgers. Rushworth and Unsworth, both failed to "come off," but B.Crompton and I.Bowen made a really excellent stand. No less than 72 runs came f om this partnership of which the first named scored 39, and his partner 33. At this point the total was 151 for five, and 34 more runs were added by Duck- worth, Woods, and Proud. At the close of the innings nine wickets had fallen for 199 runs. This fine result was very largely contributed to by the homosters who allowed no less than 27 extras. Had the match been closer they might have had cause to keenly regret their comparative inefficiency behind the stumps.

At Gorsey-lane, Warrington, another League ?fixture came off, the combatants being St. Elphin'S and Che- shire Lines Engineers. Contrary to expectation the Engineers, who went in first, could only make a weak stand against the St. Elphin's bowlers, Duckworth and Gresty. When only 25 runs had been scored half the team was out, and the remaining five only just man- aged to exceed this figure by raising the total to 58. St. Elphins tlaen went to the wickets, and it was thought that perhaps Monks and Harrison would be equally successful with the ball. They did by no means badly, but Scarisbrick,Duckworth and Barnes,made two-figured scores and with fair batting from the rdmainder a total of 80 runs was compiled. Duckworth had the best score, Barnes having the misfortune to be run out when he felt about equal to reaching last week's figure.

It has fallen to the lot of the Y.M.C.A. tear to per- form the meritorious feat of giving the Brewery eleven its first " "for this season. Much credit thus at- taches to the" Young men" who have done so badly in their previous engagements. No doubt, few of the Brewers had any idea of thero being a possibility of de- feat when they entered the Y.M.C.A. grouad,but the un- expected has happened once again. The visitors did very badly against the bowling of Howard, Woods, and Thompson and though they had their usual team on, they were all out for 30 runs. Howard took 4 wickets for two runs. When the homesters went in tbey had a fair chance of victory,and batting cautiously, they won the match by a majority of 14 runs. Heesom had the top score of 12 runs.

Sankey Wire Mills recorded still another victory cn Saturday afternoon:when the team from Hough Green came to Sankey. The visitors were all dismissed for 28 runs. Simpson and Hobson being deserving of praise for their fine bowling on behalf of the homesters. The victors themselves did not perform anything remarkable in the batting line, but they succeeded in putting to- gether 57 runs. Cooke scored 13, and his was the only individual performance of any merit.

Another match in which low scoring was the prom- inent feature was that between St. Luke's and Holy Trinity on the ground of the former. The homesters only compiled 53, of which total 21 fell from the bat of Mather, and extras 9. Holy Trinity could not do even this much for the whole team only knocked up the same number of runs as Mather, aforementioned. The brothers Ray were responsible tor this by their excellent bowling. Tho Trinitarians ha.,-1 a strong team too for it included the p'aers who formerly composed Messrs. Richmond and Co's. eleven.

div.head: FIRST PNEUMATIC TYRE,
div.p: THE FIRST PNEUMATIC TYRE,

Most people are probably aware (says" Engineering") that Mr. Dunlop was anticipated in his invention of the pneumatic tyre by a Mr. William Thompson, who took out a patent for the device about 1846. The curious thing, and one which is less generally known,is that the invention was very thoroughly tested, and shown to have great advantages, so far as the reduction of trac- tive resistance is concerned, over the tyres ordinarily in use. Thus, in the "Mechanic's Magazine " of March 27,1847,an accuunt is given of a number of experiments made in the presence of the editor of that journal,which conclusively showed the superiority of the pneumatic system. A car fitted with the pneumatic wheels was drawn over a length of road in Regent's Park,half of the distance passed over being firm and smooth, and the remainder covered with newly-broken stone. The tractive resistance on the smooth portion of the road was 23 lbs. with the pneumatic wheels, and 45 lbs. with ordinary wheels. On the newly-maca- damised portion of the road the pneumatic wheels showed a tractive resistance of 381- lbs. and the ordin- ary tyres one of 120 lbs. It was also shown that the wheels stood wear very well, as the car with which the experiments were made had been driven more than 1,200 miles over every kind of road, the wheels remain- ing in excellent condition. These wheels had an inner tube of soft rubber, and an outer one of leather, to take the wear; but in 1849 the leather was replaced by rub- ber, which was thickened on the tread, giving a tyre apparently identical in all essentials with those in use to-day. It is most remarkable that an invention so thoroughly tested, and shown to have such advantages as this, should have been allowed to lie absolutely dor- mant tor so many years. The very existence of the patent seems to have been forgotten till the re-invention of the device by Mr. Dunlop.

div.head: SINGULAR OCCURRENCE IN THE
div.p: SINGULAR OCCURRENCE IN THE
COUNTY COURT.
THROWING THE BIBLE AT A PLAINTIFF.

On Thursday afternoon at the Warrington County Court, James Albert Robinson, 21 Watkin-st., was sum- moned by his sister, Mrs. Wall, for lodgings money and monoy lent. She was stating her claim when defend- ant picked up the bible upon whieh witnesses are sworn and threw it at her. She was some distance from de- fendant and the bible missed plaintiff and struck the top of the witness-box. Judge Ffoulkes did not notice the action of defendant but Mr. Arthur Browne pointed out to him what had occurred. When the case the parties were concerned in was concluded and defendant was about to ge away, the Judge ordered him back, and committed him to gaol for seven days for contempt of Court.

Defendant was taken to the bridewell by one of the court officials and raised a great outcrf. j Lat rj, in ,the afternoon when the buliness of the court was o er Mrs. Wall went into the witness box again and told J Honour that her brother would not have done such a;Thing only he had "a sup o' beer." There was no one qbring a copper into his home and he had never been ittit court before. He had also four children. She would net like hint to go to gaol. His Honour : His offence is a very serious one. I don't know that , I can, in the interests of the public, allow such a thing to be passed over. Mrs. Wall : Well, he had a sup of beer. His Henour : lam afraid I can not let it, be passed over.
Mrs. Wall : He would not have done it but for the beer and it did not hit me.
His Honour: His conduct was such as I had never ex- perienced in my life before. I am afraid I cannot remit the punishinent, his offence is a very serious one. Mrs. Wall : I know it is.
She then left the Court looking very miserable.

div.head: REV. JOHN YONGE'S RETURN.
div.p: THE REV. JOHN YONGE'S RETURN.

The more than usually large congregation at Wycliffe Church on Sunday evening testified to the respect in which the Rev. John Yonee's townspeople generally hold him. Almost all the pewholders were present, and likewise a good sprinkling ot outsiders. The occasion was the pastor's first appearance in the pulpit -if the church since he was attacked by illness four months ago. Some members of the church, with pleasing thoughtful- ness, had placed upon the table hela cv toe pulpit, a ' collection of flowers which n• doubt doubt refreshed the preacher's eye. ' After appropriate hymns and prayer, Mr. Yo NGE said that before announcing his text he would say in one brief sentence how thankful he was to be in their midst once more. He came there that night rejoicing with trembling, believing that with God's mercy his health was coming to him once again and yet sensible that his voice is different and that his powers of making sermons were not what they might be. He had, however, the fullest confidence in the loving sympathy of all his friends. He hoPitel to take up his work amongst them by degrees. It`was suggested to him thae if he could not permanently come back he had better stop away until he could, but as he longed to see them all and trusted that such work as he might be able to do would be more acceptable than nothing, he came back that night hop- ing that strength might be gives to him to take up the various duties which belonged to his work in their midst; He then drew their attention to his text " The things; which happened un,q) me," Phillipians I. part of verse 12. 'Towards to theetid of the admirable dis- course 'which he preached freeet these words the rev. gentleman said the occasion that night was unusual , and exceptional. They and he were m 'eting again after an utterly unlooked-for separation of four months. When he left that pulpit on the evening of the 19th of April it never entered his mind that he had immediately before him a lengthened season of severe suffering, fol- lowed by weeks of exhaustion and feeblenees, and neces- sitating so protracted in absence from his work in their midst. Neither he nor they had any pre-vision of the "things which should happen to him." Therefore it was not wonderful if the uppermost thought in their ' minds, as once again they met and worshipped together, should .be of those " things which had happened." They could not do other than take the backward look that night. Most certainly he,at least, should be negli- gent if a paramount duty did he not, there and then in their midst,take a most grateful retrospect. It was but right and fitting that he sheuld make humble acknow- ledgement of thankfelness to God for the mercy which had spared his life,for the goodness which had so far re- stored to him the blessing of health. And he desired to make the acknowledgement with all the profounder feeling of gratitude because during the period of his ill- ness two of his ministerial brethren personally known to him,and one of them an old fellow-student,both of them his juniors,had passed away. They were both signally successful ministers,and up to their death in prominent service. He alluded to the Rey. Colrner Byrnes, of Ley- tonstone and the Rev. Morley Wright, of Paddington. They had been taken while he had been continued. Surely his spared life ,and his returning health were more than ever to be consecrated to Him. And he wished also to say that night that among " the things that happened to him "there had come constant and manifold displays of the goodness of God in the wonder- sul sympathy and thoughtful kindness of innumerable friends. The considerateness of their deacons in all their arrangements so as to prevent him having a single anxious care concerning that pulpit, the • messages of loving iaquiry so numerous as to be impossible of separ- ate:.acknowledgment,the almost universal sympathy of his.tellow townsmen of all sects and parties,the patience which had enabled hie people to acquiesce in his length- ened absence, the cordiality of their welcome now that he was permitted to rejoin them—all these things he did most eratefully and affectionally acknowledge. Often in his life had he had signal proof of the provi- dential care of the Father in Heaven, but he was free to say that never had that proof been so conspicuous or so manifold as in these recent months. The season of trial, of anxiety, and of physical suffering had been both pain- ful and protracted, but the comforts, the mitigations, and the compensations had been fully " according to his day." He had been the recipient of boundless living kindness, both from God and from his fellow men, and he desired to render hie most thankful acknowledgments. Hy trusted he was not saying that as a matter merely of bee,eming form. He did net find it easy to express his meaning as he should like. But if that preaching frern the pulpit was best which was straight from the preacher's own conscious experience, then they got some of it then,because from his own deep and powerful sense of it he did declare unto tbent that night the divine goodness and love. He trusted that he came back to thern with a stronger faith in the reality of the hopes and comforts of the gospel, with a fitter and richer experi- ence of them, and,therefere,it might be that he returned with some increased qualification for the work in their midst. His own feeling that night was that in the good- ness of God and by their continued confidence and affec- tion he was making a re-eornmencement, a new begin- ning of his ministry.. The many words of welcome that had been spoken to him seemed also like a renewed call to their service, and he was hoping by God's help that it would be manifestly seen ere long that the things which had happened unto him did fall out amongst them rather unto the furtherance of the gospel. When, 20 years ago, he. preached his first sermon as their pastor, his text was this—" From whence can a man satisfy these men with bread here in the wilderness ?" He answered the question then by declaring that only in the preaching of Christ, in the fulness of His divine nature, in the brotherhood of his humanity, in the sacri- fice of His atonement, and .in the inspiration of His spirit could men ever be satisfied with spiritual food. Whether he had been entirely true to the standard then put forth was hardly, perhaps, for tarn to say, but this he would venture to say, that he had endeavoured to be true. And coming back again now to that pulpit, for so long as God should keep him here his earnest desire was to preach Christ more than ever. Certain he was that no other preaching could awaken so real and deep a response. During his absence he had heard many preachers and many sermons, but none had so touched. him as those which had most set Him forth and brought his mind and heart into very touch with Him ; and now the friends, officers, and members of the Church, all their Wycliffe people, older and younger, let them use that oceasion as the opportunity of renewing former vows to Christ. It would indeed be a blessed re-ordinae tion to the ministry for him ; and a blessed welcome that they accorded him, if from that night a new spirit of devotion should take possession of all. He wanted to be spared for longer service, and he prayed to be made more manifestly useful.

div.head: STATUTORY HALF-HOLIDAY FOR DOMESTIC SERVANTS.
div.p: A STATUTORY HALF-HOLIDAY FOR DOMESTIC SERVANTS.

A few weeks ago it was cabled that the Domestic Ser- vants' fiatfJioliday Bill had received a second reading in the New Zea:and House of Representatives. Further particulars are to be had by mail. The effects of this measure are best described in the words of Lady Stout, wife of Sir Robert Stout, a former Radical Premier of New Zealand. Lady Stout is herself a prominent poli- tician and a leading figure at female congresses in that colony ; but this latest legislative proposal is somewhat teo advanced even for her. She points out that a large proportion of the servants in towns are country girls without friends, and as under the provisions of the bill they would have to be turned out of their houses from 3 p.m. until 10 p.m. on one day in every week, they would have no alternative but to parade the streets. They could not even return to their own houses during the statutory hours for food unless their mistresses consented to wait upon them, as the mistress was liable to a penalty of k:,5 if the servants were employed at their ordinary work when they ought to enjoy their statutory halt- holiday. Lady Stout thinks it would be better to pass a law granting a weekly half-holidays to mothers of families who have no servants, but who have to work night and day the whole year round. She would compel her husband to remain at home and mind the house on ' these occassions.

div.head: PRACTICAL SOCIALIg3I IN MTZER-
div.p: PRACTICAL SOCIALIg3I IN MTZER-
LAND.

Mr. Jesse Macy contributes to the" American Journal of Sociology "for July a very interesting sketch of" The Swiss and their Politics." Mr. Macy was delighted to find the Swiss so much in advance of the American in al that relates to the control of plutocracy by the people. Intelligent Swiss with whom he talked were amazed at the extent to which the country of George Washington was dominated by the power of the purse, Yet there is no Socialism in Switzerland excepting tliats%ie prac- tical kind, some illustrati..?ns of which Mr. Macy cribes the flollotvinep*lsage er— I have-been surptlind;at the cool au, •i.,.,..1r-Of-fact way in which the Swiss, through their governmental agencies, assume control of industrial operations which Americans regard as belonging to private enterprise. The Swiss were among the first to.adopt the government telegraph. This suited them so well that when the tele- phone had fully demonstrated its usefulness, without any special debate or fuss about the matter, theritade the telephone an integral part of the' postal-telegiaphic system. For about 9dols. one has the utie of it tele- phone for a year,with connections in all parts of the city and country. They have a pareels post which corre- sponds to our express business. It cost me 5 cents to send by mail my manuscript on the English Government from one end of Switzerland to the other. For a like service in the United States mail I think I have paid 75 cents. It is only recently that measures have been adopted looking to the govern- ment ownership of all the railways in Switzerland, and I have been completely dumbfounded at the apparent lack of interest in the subject. The government has recently taken charge of the manufacture and sale of matches. I think the Government monopoly of the sale of alcohol drink has excited more debate. But the point of interest has been the suppression of drunken- ness rather than the industrial effects. There is now a measure before the national legislation for establishing a national bank, and this is causing some newspaper dis- cussion.
In the cantons and in the cities there are movements of a similar character, Various cantons anvi communes have in recent years assumed the burden of burying the dead.

While I was in Geneva, the city gained possession of the lighting plant of an outlying district which had pre- viously been in the hands of a company. A few years ago the city began to utilize the power of the Rhone river, which comes out of the lake in a mighty torrent. They needed the water of the lake in their streets and houses, and they made the river pump the water. The watch industry was languishing on account or competi- tion with the machine-made watch in America and else- where. The city eorporation developed a system for dis- tributing power to the local manufacturers through the pressure of water pumped from the Rhone by the Rhone. This gave a great stimulus to many industries, and more power was demanded. When experience had demon- strated the economy of electricity as an agency for lighting and for the distribution of power the city gained possession of all electrical appliances and attached them to their mill on the Rhone. lity all these demands the power of the river as developed within the city limits was exhausted, and the demand for power to be used in manufacture was rapidly increasing. To meet the new demand the city government secured a site four miles down the river, where they have constructed a dam ot stone which ap- pears as permanent as Niagara Falls, and where they get an immense head of water. This new mill is now nearing completion. From it power will be distributed by electricity and sold to small manufacturers in the city and suburbs. On my return to the city from my visit to the new mill I rode with a manufacturer from Zurich. Ile said that their company bought power from a private company, and that they paid 3 dol. for power which costs the Genevese manufacturer only 2 dol.

The surprising thing about the matter i the cool and matter-of-fact way in which the government enters upon these various industrial undertakings. A few days before I left Geneva the city government voted to build at once twelve tenement houses to be owned and operated by the city. It was understood that this was only the beginning of an enterprise which admitted of infinite expansion. There is probably no part of Europe where the socialists are having so hard a time as in Switzerland.

div.head: DEFICIT ON THE YEAR'S WORKING.
div.p: A DEFICIT ON THE YEAR'S WORKING.

The balance-sheet of the above union has just been published, and is an interesting document in more ways than one. On the summary of receipts and payments £732 63. 6d. has been turned over altogether, and gates at the respective matches were taken as follows: Cheshire v. Lancashire, at Stockport, £5l 18s. id.; Y. ra4iire v. Cheshire, at Leeds, £55 63. ; Lanca- shire v. Yorkshire, at Oldham, £274 17g.; Lancs.- shire v. Cheshire, at Broughton, £94 124. lid.; Cheshire v. Yorkshire, at Runcorn, £44 183. ; York-- shire v. Lancashire, at Huddersfield, £llB ss. 6d. The expenses in connection with these matches were heavy, and in two instances actually exceeded the receints. The cost of the Lancashire v. Yorkshire match was £l6l 193. 3d, but after this contest there was an expensive dinner which is not likely Ls be repeated. County caps cost £53, jerseys £4B 103 ; and on the year's working generally there is a deficit of £96 9.3, 10d. The general meeting is to be held at Hud- dersfield on Thursday next, the 27th inst., at ball-past five and several important proposals are on the agenda. The chief one is regarding the government of the union, and as to this the committee themselves will propose as follows ;--" The union to be governed by a commit-- the of thirty members. The following clubs (as founders of the union)—viz.. Bradford, Brighouse Rangers, Bat- ley, Broughton Rangers, Halifax, Hunslet, Hull, Hud- dersfield ,Liversedge,Leeds,Leigh, Manningham,Oldham. Rochdale Hornets, Runcorn, St. Helens, Stockport, Tyl- desley, Wakefield Trinity, Warrington, Wigan, and Widnes, shall ;each be entitled to elect one representa- tive so long as such clubs retain their position in the front rank of Rugby football. The remaining eight seats shall be distributed to other counties or districts- as necessity arises,at the discretion of the committee."
J. H. DUTTON,

GREAT SANKEY PARISM COUNCIL.—A meeting of the members of this Council was convened for. Monday evening, and there were present, Messrs. H. Bate (in tbe chair), T. Halton, G. Thompson, W. E. L. Gorse, W. Taylor, and J. Wright, (cleric). .After the minutes had been read, Mr. Thompson objected to the validity of the nseeting on the ground that it was not held at a time fixed by a resolution of the Council. After some discussion this objection was upheld by the Chairman, and consequently no business was transacted.

A serious accident attended Tuesday's yachting, in the Southsea regatta. Two competitions, for craft of differ- ent sizes,were in progress,and,by an unexpected turn of events,the competitors were all rounding a mark at the same time. As far as can be gathered, the Isolde was trying to avoid a foul with the Prince of Wales's yaeht Britannia, when The Saint struck lair backstay and forced her round on the German Emperor's yacht Meteor. These two came into such violent collision that the Isolde was virtually wrecked, and all on board were swept into the water, including the owner, Baron von Zodtwitz.who was also terribly injured by the fall of the mainsail from. A number of rowing boats were put out, the crew were quickly got out of the water, but Baron von Zedtwitz died from his injuries directly after- wards.
